As the hon. member realizes, this results in higher costs for the Canadian consumer, for shoes, for textiles, for food or whatever it is. Because of this, Mr. Speaker, it is important that, while we take these protective measures, we also take steps to ensure that these industries become more modern and more cost efficient so that they can compete in world markets and therefore will not need the artificial protection of trade barriers, which seems to be the policy of the hon. member.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: DAIRY FARMERS-MINISTER'S STATEMENT
speechtext:
1. No-The
Minister of Agriculture has not said that all dairy farmers are "greedy". He has said on a number of occasions that a minority of fluid milk producers are greedy for not wanting to share the burden of surplus and over-production with industrial milk producers. The expansion of some fluid milk operations at the expense of industrial milk producers does not display a Christian attitude. In his discussions with dairy farmers at their meetings, government policy as well as the minister's personal views have been explained very carefully to those present.
2.	Yes-As a practising farmer, the minister is well aware of the hours of work required for all farmers, not just dairy farmers and that their motivation is the same as other people. Farmers are very capable of making their views known to the minister and their exchange of views with the minister keeps him up-to-date at all times.

subsubtopic: FUNDS FOR CRIME PREVENTION
speechtext:
1.	Will there be an infusion of funds into crime prevention for better trained, deployed and equipped policemen and, if so (a) in what amounts (b) for what purposes?
2.	Were funds or man-years made available to the RCMP as a result of the introduction of the peace and security legislation and, if so, what were they?
3.	Have additional RCMP positions been allotted to do the administrative work on the new gun law proposals and, if so, how many?

subsubtopic: FUNDS FOR CRIME PREVENTION
speechtext:
1. Funds have been made available under the Peace and Security program to strengthen existing capabilities in crime prevention. In collaboration with provincial and municipal authorities and an advisory board, which includes representatives from the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police and the RCMP, emphasis is being placed on providing police with practical, innovative,
2096

January 23, 1978
Order Paper Questions
community-oriented preventive programs which address local needs. Although many of these programs, such as Operation Identification, Neighbourhood Watch and Block Parents depend upon active voluntary community support, some, such as team policing, involve changes in the deployment of a city's force and may involve additional training as well as equipment. While funds were not specifically provided for better trained police officers, there is some concern to ensure that policing in general, and police recruit and in-service training in particular, come to reflect a more even balance between law enforcement and preventive policing. To this end, it is felt that some orientation in family crisis intervention and similar programs should, where appropriate, be made available to police forces and training establishments, (a) $1,108,000 for 1976/ 77. (b) For developing, disseminating and implementing model prescriptive policing packages.
2.	No specific resources were made available to the RCMP as a result of the introduction of the Peace and Security legislation but while man-year growth in the government as a whole was kept below 1 per cent during 1976-77, the RCMP increased by 4.4 per cent. Of the net increase in man-years authorized for departments and agencies whose man-years are subject to Treasury Board control, 14.7 per cent were allotted to the RCMP. Financial resources granted to the RCMP were also allowed to exceed the average increase for all government departments and agencies, for the same year. These increases were in recognition of the priority the government attached to innovative measures in crime control (Peace and Security).
3.	No man-years have as yet been allotted to the RCMP by Treasury Board. It is anticipated however, that seven man-years will be provided for the fiscal year 1977/78.

2.	(a) What services or programmes are available through the National Film Board to elementary and secondary school teachers (b) by province, what was the cost for such services in each of the past five years?

subsubtopic: NFB-POLICY ON USE OF AUDIO-VISUAL TAPES, FILMS AND SCRIPTS IN ELEMENTARY AND SECONDARY SCHOOLS
speechtext:
I am informed by the National Film Board as follows: 1. It is the policy of the National Film Board to promote and assist in the development of audio-visual services to Canadian schools and teachers and to support their operations and growth with its own productions and resources, rather than to substitute for the education system in providing such services. The production and resources of the National Film Board reach elementary and secondary schools in Canada in many ways: (1) All productions distributed by the National Film Board are made available in 16mm format on a free loan basis to elementary and secondary schools, usually through the established audio-visual service of the school or the schools system. The same productions are also available for purchase from the National Film Board offices across the country. Such purchases can often be made at varying discounted rates on quantity orders and/or within a film library development programme. (2) Where such capabilities exist, departments of education or provincial telecommunication authorities can purchase from the National Film Board the rights to broadcast within the educational television system or closed-circuit school TV system, to transfer from film to tape and to reproduce quantity of tapes of all productions cleared for such distribution. In addition, the National Film Board now sells all such productions on tape format. (3) Other audio-visual products, such as 8mm films, filmstrips, slides presentation, transparencies, multi-media kits, are available for purchase by schools from three (3) distributors in the country. (4) It is not the policy of the National Film Board to provide scripts of its productions although in a few instances such scripts have been made available free of charge for film studies.
2. There is no service provided by the National Film Board specifically designed for teachers in the elementary and secondary schools. This is considered to be the responsibility of the departments and boards of education. However, like any other Canadian, the elementary and secondary school teachers have access to the free loan service from the National Film Board 27 film libraries across the country. speechtext:

(a) What is the procedure followed in the hiring by the government of Canadian teachers to teach at Canadian Armed Forces bases overseas (b) how many are employed (c) what is the salary scale (d) what is the amount of foreign service allowance awarded (e) what provisions are made for (i) travel expenses (ii) medical insurance coverage?

speakeroldname: Mr. Yvon Pinard (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: CONDITIONS OF EMPLOYMENT OF TEACHERS OVERSEAS
speechtext:
I am informed by the Department of National Defence, the Chief Electoral Office and Revenue Canada as follows:
1.	(a) Teachers for overseas DND dependants schools are obtained from their employing school boards in Canada under a two-year loan-of-service agreement. Interested applicants apply to their employing board for such an assignment. The board reviews all applications received and forwards suitable nominations to the Department of National Defence. The National

Defence Headquarters Teachers Selection Committee makes the final selection, (b) 296 (including direction, administrative and teaching staffs), (c) The employing board continues to pay the salary authorized under their salary agreement whilst the teacher is assigned overseas. The department reimburses the board for monthly salary payments made, (d) Foreign service allowance for teachers is calculated in the same manner as for members of the Canadian Forces and the amount may fluctuate according to the cost of living or post indices established by Statistics Canada. Other factors that have an influence are salary entitlements, length of service overseas and whether the teacher is accompanied by dependants. The minimum and maximum allowances now vary between approximately $300 to $700 per month, (e) (i) Teachers are entitled to travelling allowances as though proceeding on duty as a member of the Canadian Forces, (ii) Teachers are covered for adequate hospital-medical insurance under provincial health insurance plans, where extended outside Canada, or under the Canadian Teachers Association in Europe (CTAE) Group Plan, a health care plan sponsored by the Canadian Premier Life Insurance Company.
2.	The provisions of the recently amended Special Voting Rules (Schedule II to the Canada Elections Act) include provisions for the taking of the votes, at a general election, of Canadian Forces electors, including teachers and administrative support staff at Canadian Forces schools outside Canada, and their eligible dependants residing with them.
3.	Members of the Canadian Forces (as well as employees of all Canadian departments) are deemed residents of Canada pursuant to paragraph 250(1 )(b) of the Income Tax Act. Any foreign service allowance received by such members is specifically exempted from tax under subparagraph 6(l)(b)(iii) of the Act. School teachers are subject to tax under subsection 115(2) of the act and there is no similar provision exempting teachers from paying tax on foreign service allowance. However, in order to rectify this anomalous situation a remission order, titled "Department of National Defence Overseas School Staff Income Tax Remission Order 1976", permits a teacher to elect to be taxed as though he was a member of the Canadian Forces. Therefore, if a teacher makes the election there will be a remission of federal income tax which was paid on the foreign service allowance. subsubtopic: TORUTEIN
speechtext: Is Torutein, manufactured by Amoco Foods Company in the United States, a torula yeast grown on pure alcohol and do advertisements for the product claim that it replaces milk solids, improves meat flavour and binds fats and water, replaces dried egg yolks, imparts a smooth mouthfeel and enhances sour cream flavour and, if so (a) what tests have been done by the Health Protection Branch, Food and Drug Administration or the Company to indicate that this product is safe for human consumption (b) what tests have been done to indicate that Torutein, which is used to replace milk solids and egg yolks, provides the same nourishment (c) under what regulations is the product being sold in Canada and are there any regulations which would limit its use in food products?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: TORUTEIN
speechtext:
Torutein, manufactured by Amoco Foods, is a Torula yeast (Candida utilis) which is grown on food grade ethyl alcohol, using a continuous aseptic fermentation process. The yeast is grown as a pure culture under controlled conditions designed to give uniform products. The yeast is continuously harvested, concentrated by centrifugation, pasteurized, spray dried, and bagged using sanitary processes as normally found in the dry milk industry. The advertisements for Torutein do claim that its use improves meat flavour; binds fats and water; imparts a smooth mouthfeel; enhances sour cream flavour in dressings, sauces and dips; and partially replaces non-fat dry milk and eggs, for functional and organoleptic purposes, in certain unstandardized baking formulas, (a) Amoco Foods Company had done chemical, microbiological, nutritional and toxicological studies on Torutein, and the results of these studies indicate that the product per se is safe for human consumption, (b) Data provided by the manufacturer indicate that the nutritional quality of TTorutein differs from that of dried egg yolk and milk solids. It is higher in protein although of a lower nutritional quality and contains higher levels of B vitamins except vitamin B12 and folic acid. Its total mineral content is comparable to that of milk solids but it contains negligible amounts of calcium and more magnesium and iron, (c) Torula yeast has been used as a Food ingredient for a considerable period of time. Although there are no regulations controlling the sale of the product per se, its sale as a food or food ingredient is subject to the general provisions of the Food and Drugs Act relating to safety and lack of deception. Torutein may be used as an ingredient in unstandardized foods. While there are no legal limitations on its level of use in these foods, its upper use level is self-limiting at around 3 per cent due to undesirable colour, texture and yeasty taste. Most staple foods are subject to standards of composition in the Food and Drug Regulations which specify the ingredients which may be used in those foods. The Health Protection Branch policy has been to consider Torutein used in condimental proportions to be "seasoning", and therefore its use has been permitted in those standardized foods for which provision is made for "seasoning". The addition of Torutein in condimental proportions to standardized foods should not replace any nutritive ingredient. If Torutein were used in higher than condimental proportions as a replacement for nutritious ingredients, a different set of circumstances would exist. It is the policy of the Department of National Health
Order Paper Questions
and Welfare to ensure that substitution of ingredients does not decrease the nutritional quality of the diet. For example, regulations were recently promulgated requiring that any protein sources added to meat and poultry products to extend the protein or used to simulate meat or poultry products contain protein and vitamins and mineral nutrients in amounts equivalent to those found in meat. Torutein used in more than condimental proportions in meat or poultry products would be subject to these regulations. The development of such regulations is an ongoing process in response to the development of new foods.

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION ACT
speechtext:
1.	From what specific section or subsection of the Financial Administration Act was the mandate of the Planning Branch, Treasury Board Secretariat derived?
2.	What were the initial terms of reference of the Planning Branch?
3.	Was the Planning Branch supposed to concern itself with reviewing existing policies and programmes or with analysing proposed policies and programmes?
4.	Of the 733 man-years allocated to the Treasury Board for planning and evaluation activities since the 1970-71 estimates, how many man-years have been devoted to ensuring that money is spent with due regard to economy and efficiency?
5.	How many man-years have been devoted to ensuring that programmes are effective and that the desired results and benefits of the programme are being achieved?
6.	What projects have been undertaken by the Planning Branch since 1970-71 in fulfilling its mandate?
7.	Which of these projects have been concerned with ensuring that programmes are effective and that the desired results and benefits of the programmes are being achieved?
8.	Did the Planning Branch undertake studies which led to the decision to disband Information Canada, the Company of Young Canadians or the Local Initiatives Programme?
9.	Has the mandate of the Planning Branch been changed recently?
10.	Why was the Organization Division and the Task Force on Decentralization shifted from the Planning Branch to the Programme Branch?
11.	Why were the Effectiveness Evaluation Division and the Performance Measurement Policy Division elevated to branch status?

12.	Does the Planning Branch presently concern itself with the review of existing policies and programmes or the analysis of proposed policies or programmes?
13.	Does the Efficiency Evaluation Branch presently concern itself with the review of existing policies and programmes or the analysis of proposed policies or programmes?
14.	Are any of the planning and evaluation studies undertaken by the Efficiency Evaluation Branch used in the budgeting process?
15.	Are any of the planning and evaluation studies undertaken by the Planning Branch used in the budgeting process?
16.	Are any of the planning and evaluation studies undertaken by the Efficiency Evaluation Branch done in cooperation with the Auditor General?
17.	Are any of the planning and evaluation studies undertaken by the Planning Branch done in cooperation with the Auditor General?
18.	What will be the relationship between the proposed Comptroller General and the Planning Branch?
19.	What will be the relationship between the proposed Comptroller General and the Efficiency Evaluation Branch?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION ACT
speechtext:
1. The mandate of the planning branch of the Treasury Board Secretariat was derived from section 5(1) (c) and 5(1) (d) of the Financial Administration Act.
2.	The initial terms of reference of the planning branch were to initiate and undertake studies of the effectiveness of selected government programmes and the efficiency of selected administrative units and, as techniques and methods of evaluation are developed, to transmit them to departments.
3.	The planning branch was not restricted to studying proposed or existing policies and programmes. It could both review existing policies and programmes and analyse proposed policies and programmes.
4.	Twenty-five man-years were budgeted each year since the 1970-71 estimates for the study of economy and efficiency by the performance measurement policy division.
5.	Forty-eight man-years were budgeted each year for the effectiveness evaluation division to ensure that programmes are effective and that the desired results and benefits of the programmes are being achieved.
6.	The information requested refers to internal departmental projects of a confidential nature and cannot be released.
7.	The information requested refers to internal departmental projects of a confidential nature and cannot be released.
8.	The planning branch did not undertake studies which led to the decision to disband Information Canada, the Company of Young Canadians or the Local Initiatives Programme.
9.	Yes, the mandate of the planning branch has recently been changed.
10.	The organization division and the task force on decentralization shifted from the planning branch to the programme branch to rationalize the resource reallocation process.
11.	The organizational status of the performance measurement policy division has not been changed. It is a division within a new branch called the efficiency evaluation branch. In addition to being responsible for the board's performance measurement policy work, the new branch is responsible for
January 23, 1978

policies governing procedures for evaluation of programmes by departments.
12.	The planning branch currently concerns itself with both the review of existing policies and programmes and the analysis of proposed policies and programmes.
13.	The role of the efficiency evaluation branch is to develop and ensure the application of policies, procedures and practices to evaluate and report upon the efficiency and effectiveness of government programmes. The branch is therefore concerned with ensuring that there are appropriate policies and procedures concerning performance measurement and programme evaluation. The branch does not review or analyze existing and proposed policies and programmes.
14.	As noted in the response to question 13, the efficiency evaluation branch does not conduct planning and evaluation studies of programmes. However, the two policies for which it is responsible, performance measurement and program evaluation procedures, do relate to the budgeting process. One of the requirements of the performance measurement policy is that measures of the performance of programs be supplied by departments, where feasible, in support of their annual resource allocation requests. The policy governing evaluation of programmes by departments provides for the Treasury Board to participate in such evaluations, where this would be of use in arriving at resource allocation decisions. There is a constant liaison between the efficiency evaluation branch and the programme branch in this work.
15.	Yes, the programme branch use planning branch studies in the budgeting process.
16.	A close liaison has been established between the Study of Procedures in Cost Effectiveness (SPICE) team of the Officer of the Auditor General and the efficiency evaluation branch. This liaison is to assist SPICE in carrying out its study. A joint review of the "procedures" used for measuring the performance of the income security programme of the Department of National Health and Welfare was carried out by SPICE and efficiency evaluation branch staffs. There are also frequent exchanges of information of techniques for carrying out these reviews of procedures.
17.	No, there are no planning and evaluation studies undertaken by the planning branch in cooperation with the Auditor General.
18.	As with the rest of the Treasury Board secretariat, all planning branch material will be available to the Comptroller General.
19.	The President of Treasury Board plans to transfer the efficiency evaluation branch to the Comptroller General following passage of the legislation establishing the Comptroller General.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that in March of this year the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald), introduced a bill to amend sections 6 of the Bank Act and Quebec Savings Banks Act to permit the banks incorporated under those acts to continue to carry on business until March 31, 1978, nine months beyond the date specified. The short bill before us today will further extend the banks' powers to do business until March 31, 1979.
The reasons given in March for the delay in the decennial revision were the following. First, the extent of consultations encouraged by the white paper. Second, the extent and complexity of the task of converting the principles of white paper into legislation and particularly, where appropriate, making the Bank Act consistent with the principles and provisions of the Canada Business Corporations Act and, third, the extent of the pressure of other priorities on the small group of legislative drafters in the Department of Justice.
The consultative process based on the white paper has largely ended but the other two reasons have continued to be a source of delay. However, I am now able to report that the preparation of the legislation is nearing completion and the bill will soon be ready for introduction. This bill will result in an extensively remodelled Bank Act, important amendments to
[Mrs. Holt.)
the Quebec Savings Bank Act, amendments to the Bank of Canada Act and the Bills of Exchange Act, and will establish the statutory framework for the creation of the Canadian payments association. It is my minister's intention to introduce this legislation as soon as possible in this session.
The package of legislation I have just described will, of necessity, be long and complex, reflecting, with some changes, the proposals of the white paper on banking legislation. To ensure that parliament will be able to debate the issues unimpeded by a time constraint, and to resolve any uncertainty about the life of the existing act, we are proposing that parliament should proceed immediately with the bill to extend further the powers of the banks to do business.
The bill is quite straightforward, extending the banking powers to March 31, 1979, and reintroducing the wording of sections 6 of both acts as it was prior to the amendment earlier this year. That wording provides flexibility and acts as a safeguard in the event that parliament is not sitting at the end of March, 1979, and has not by then passed the general revision legislation or a further extension bill.
As indicated, we will bring forth the comprehensive banking legislation as soon as possible, and we look forward to full and useful committee consideration and debate.
We assure hon. members that the objectives remain those set out in the government's white paper, that is, to provide for a fair and responsive evolution of Canada's payments system, recognizing the growing importance of near-banks in the financial transactions of the nation; to provide more reasonable rules for the entry of new institutions into banking, or the conversion of existing institutions into banks; to deal with the question of foreign-owned banking institutions in Canada; to deal in detail with the business and corporate powers of the banks.
In all of these areas the goal is to encourage more competition in Canadian banking, while keeping control of our banking and financial system in Canadian hands.
We are confident that these goals are supported by all sides in this House. The extension bill will guarantee us the opportunity to give the new, comprehensive legislation which is to follow the full debate and scrutiny it deserves.
speakername: Mr.   Ed. Lumley@Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to show any disrespect for the parliamentary secretary, he is a pleasant enough chap, but I think that we on this side of the House feel that the government is now showing its traditional incompetence and laissez faire attitude in dealing with this legislation. We are now in the opening day of the resumed session, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien)-who privately had indicated to me his great desire to get through this bill and told me he hoped he would be able to table for first reading the government's proposals to amend the Bank Act by the Christmas adjournment or, if not, shortly thereafter-chooses-and the choice is his because he makes his out of city appointments as he sees fit-not to be here today. All I can say is that the debate is going to be longer
January 23, 1978

than shorter because I do not think we should handle parliament that way.
With all due respect to the parliamentary secretary, I know he was handed a high smelling basket on this occasion and it is not his fault, but, frankly, I had hoped, when I discussed this first with the Minister of Finance, that he would agree to one speech from each representative of the parties, if need be, and that we should then go into committee of the whole House to amend the motion. I still hope we can amend the motion so that this one paragraph bill does not go to committee and through all the weighty business of the legislative process that flows from that, and that we can dispose of the bill in a matter of an hour and a half in the House. That is what should be done with a bill of this kind, but the circumstances have changed, and my caucus colleagues have convinced me that we should act otherwise.
The revisions of the Bank Act, such as they are today, do not have the same high profile that the 1976-77 revisions had. At that time there was a statutory ceiling on interest rates, there were user charges and minimum balances, and there was the question of foreign ownership. In other words, the Bank Act was strictly out of kilter with business conditions. At that time people were feeling pretty excited about the Bank Act. At the present time there is not that high profile in the general community with regard to banks. Despite this lower profile in the mind of the public there is a very great and urgent need in the business community-and there has been for a long time- for a more up-to-date system of financial institutions. The structure has to be changed.
I remember back in 1972 or 1973 telling the former minister of finance, Mr. Turner, that he should set up a royal commission on banking and financial requirements in Canada, bearing in mind the great increase in the importance of banks. This had been a question in the sixties. The 1966-67 revision was a second go around following the Porter commission report. The government had come up with an atrocious bill. The Porter commission was based on statistics of the late 1950s and early 1960's and on operations based on the 1954 revision.
There has been a fantastic change in business operations and requirements for financing in Canada. It is almost as though we have moved an age in light years. However, the government did not see fit to set up an inquiry and, frankly our Bank Act is totally out of date with our requirements, to the detriment of economic activity in this country. I do not care whether it is for a small operator or a large multinational corporation; our Bank Act is totally out of date. Chartered banks are into all kinds of activities, but they would like to be into many more in a different form.
What I find more disconcerting than anything else are the activities which are beyond the control of the Minister of Finance and the review of the Inspector General of Banks. Let us consider the operations of the so-called satchel, or suitcase, bankers. They represent foreign business interests. They are able to drop into hotel rooms for a week or two weeks in
Bank Act
Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver or anywhere else, and carry on their operations. They are able to sign up substantial sums of Canadian savings, Finance, make bridge loans, provide intermediate financing or engage in supplementary lines of credit. They can do a number of things. They are not every-day banking operations which cash cheques, open savings accounts, sell travellers cheques and provide traditional over-the-counter banking services. These services are provided by chartered banks, but we also see them provided at credit unions and caisses populaires. There are national and provincial trust companies which also carry on the business of banking, and that to me is the key.
Under the British North America Act the Government of Canada is assigned exclusive jurisdiction over money and banking. I suggest that this is one item in the constitution which is distinguished by its breach 24 hours a day. There are credit unions, caisses populaires and trust companies which carry on the business of banking without any supervision whatever and with total disregard for the monetary policies set down by the Minister of Finance in the discharge of his legal responsibilities. He has no control over them. Our economy is going along on a lopsided pace because of that. If there are rules and guidelines for those who engage in the business of banking, I think they should be complied with.
I said ten or 15 years ago that there is no jurisdiction residing in a provincial government over the conduct of the business of banking, or what is called the quasi business of banking, simply because institutions conducting these operations are incorporated under some form of provincial legislation. One might as well say that because provincial governments have the conduct of the policies and operations of provincial trust companies because they are incorporated under charters issued under the corporation laws of the provinces, in the same way those provincial governments could say to companies carrying on the business of flying by charter or by schedule that "we will lay down the rules with regard to the air operations of your company, the conditions for issuing licences for aircraft and licences for your personnel, et cetera" simply because those companies are incorporated under provincial corporation laws. To me you cannot have it both ways.
I know that one of the problems with the delay in this legislation has to do with the first of the proposals contained in the white paper dealing with a Canadian payments system whereby provincial governments and credit unions are not agreeing to pay the freight to belong to a Canadian payments system. They want all the benefits without assuming any of the obligations. If they want to engage in the business of banking, they should assume the obligations, but the procedure adopted by the government of the day through the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp), who was then minister of finance, and under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act of the 1960's, was to seek the consent or approval of the provinces to set up such a system. The door was opened wide and, of course, there is very much co-operation and so forth.

January 23, 1978
Bank Act
When the shoe is on the other foot and the government moves into an area of exclusive provincial jurisdiction, it often takes little time for some of the provinces to say, "Keep your cotton picking hands off and stay out." I wish they would sometimes observe that in reverse.
The Bank Act expired on June 30, 1977. It was extended by Bill C-39 passed by this House last April, which is to expire on March 31 next. A rather complicated formula was included in the bill. I would have preferred an extension to July 1, bearing in mind what appeared to be some reluctance on the part of the President of Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) to do anything about the white paper as far as the standing committee was concerned, but the compromise was made for March 31, 1978. The effective date now, therefore, is March 31, 1979, and if parliament is not sitting at that time a formula date is to be decided by this House and the other place.
At the conclusion of this debate I will ask the parliamentary secretary to level with this House. I know that one of the considerations is the report of the commission on corporate concentration. When the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) was minister of finance he was always being asked when that was coming forward. Why talk about issuing a white paper when, if the report on corporate concentration is to be worth the paper it is written on, it will make some observations about directorates of the major financial institutions of this country? I do not prejudge that report one way or the other. It may have some very worth-while recommendations to make, but since the administration of our chartered banks and trust companies is of such material import it does not seem to have been worth publishing the white paper of August, 1976. Is it to be thrown in the waste basket because subsequent recommendations are more valid? I have never been able to follow this government's thinking, Mr. Speaker.
This procrastination goes all the way back to the former minister of finance, Mr. Turner. It may have been that his hands were tied by the fact that this government was in a minority position between 1972 and 1974 and was unwilling even to crack a smile for fear it might be thought to be prejudiced. After 1974, when there was a growing unease between the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the then minister of finance which culminated in a banging door- "Comme on dit en claquant les portes" resignation by the minister and the appointment of the hon. member for Rosedale as minister of finance, we were into the swim of wage and price controls.
During all of this time the other place was able to consider the contents of the white paper and received representations from interested parties which were of limited value. I am going to suggest that when and if the bill incorporating the amendments to the new Bank Act come in, hon. members of the other place will have to go through the whole process again because conditions will have changed.
Knowing some of the background, it seems to me that the white paper was not referred to the Standing Committee on

Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs because of the unwillingness of the then minister of finance and the government House leader to have a lengthy debate. The opposition was asked to agree to a quick referral of the white paper and then, if the government brought in the bill, to agree that the second reading would be pro forma and the contents of the bill superimposed on the white paper. I never heard of such a mish-mash in my life, Mr. Speaker, and I would have no part of it.
This points out the total inadequacy and the lunatic system of committees that we have in this House whereby legislation and estimates are referred to standing committees. At times the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs may have half a dozen bills lined up, as well as the estimates for many departments and agencies. It is by far the busiest committee on average.
It is my view that, in the consideration of estimates, parliament's job is the examination and provision of supply as soon as the blue book on estimates comes down. This year that may occur next week or in the early part of February, but the guillotine falls on May 31. No legislation should go through any committee under this system. A change has been offered to the House but people are frightened of change. There is no way a white paper or Bank Act should be prevented from being referred to a committee on banking-a committee which would die after it accomplished its work. As things stand, the government will not get second reading of the bill and consideration by the committee before May 31.
Let us examine the sequence, Mr. Speaker. There will be a debate on Second reading and at that time members on both sides of the House will be heard in extenso because banking is so important. It is twelve years since banking was discussed in depth in this House so we can expect an extended debate. Then there will be public hearings.
It takes a matter of six weeks at least between the reception of a report and the commencement of public hearings. Notices have to be published across the country inviting representations and, depending upon the public reaction, it may be that the hearings will take longer than anticipated. The committee then makes a report which may have some extensive changes. The government has to take time to consider those recommendations and either at committee stage, or the report stage, bring in a whole series of amendments which will occasion debate; and on it goes.
It is a long process, but the act is one of the most important ones we have on the statute books. Mr. Speaker, I cannot foresee that even in an off election year that there should be a shortened process. Certainly it would be shorter if one had special legislative committees rather than just standing committees to consider estimates and legislation each vying for the necessary time. Some day there will be a revolution in some of the thinking around here with regard to our committee structure, and we will have a vehicle that will be far more effective. I am looking at the government chief whip. He knows whereof
January 23, 1978

I speak; he has seen the framework and I think he understood my purpose, but he was scared by it. He thought he had too many committees to get too many people for. He is wasting away to a shadow, literally in trying to man the committees as they now stand. We are very glad to see the congenial whip back functioning in full bore in his duties now.
Why should there be changes in the Bank Act? First of all incorporation. In the last couple of years we have had that unedifying process of trying to incorporate the Continental Bank via a private member's bill. If there ever was a more disgraceful procedure, costly, uncertain, undignified, unworthy of this House, it was the performance with regard to the Continental Bank. There are certainly proper guidelines laid down by administrative requirements with the control by the governor in council of issuing the permit to commence business after the Inspector General of Banks is satisfied that all the minimum requirements are met. There is absolutely no reason why banks should not be incorporated in the corporate affairs branch.
Then we come to the Canadian payments system. Frankly the credit unions and the trust companies in their desire to participate in the payments system strike me as people wanting to ride a bus and not wanting to pay. They want a free ride. There is no way in my book that that should happen.
And, as I mentioned earlier there are the activities of the foreign banks in Canada. I am not going to say that foreign banks are bad per se. They themselves must think it is a joke right now in the way they can operate without any supervision whatsoever; except if they establish an incorporated subsidiary and carry on from a well posted place. There are foreign controlled banks; there are foreign banks. There is a distinction.
One of the strengths of the Canadian chartered banks system is the extent to which the major Canadian banks are able to operate abroad and, to the extent that they have done so, the strength they possess in certain markets, New York for example. Now, as sure as big apples come from little apples, if the Canadian government in a moment of irresponsibility decided to clamp down and subject foreign banks to impossible conditions, the quick result would be that foreign jurisdictions, the government of the United States, or the legislature of the state involved, or any European country, or any other country in which Canadian banks operate, would retaliate, and not necessarily on a tit-for-tat basis.
There is no way that there can be a sort of punitive control imposed on foreign banks. We invite the competition, but you know right now it isn't competition. Everything is loaded against Canadian banks dealing with some foreign competitors who have no standards to meet, no expenses to meet and who can come in and offer a major line of credit at a quarter per cent or half a per cent less.
I heard of one case today where a large Canadian corporation was offered a line of credit of $60 million. They owed about maybe $200 million, that is potentially in the line of
Bank Act
credit extended to them. They were offered a line of credit of $60 million at something less than prime. Why all it took was a flying visit from a representative to call in on the board of directors a few phones calls, and maybe a lunch or two. Of course they can shave off maybe a quarter per cent, or even three eighths of a per cent. But, on $60 million, that means a lot. Fortunately the Canadian bank told its customer that if they wanted to take that line of credit that they could call up the competitor and, ask them to take on the other loan too. Nothing, of course, was heard about the whole blessed operation. But that is the sort of competition, totally unfair and irresponsible and beyond the supervision of the Inspector General of Banks.
I would like to see well defined definitions and guidelines for the conduct of merchant banking in Canada. Goodness knows how many merchant bankers there are from the United States, from Britain, France, and Germany who participate in Canada. Why shouldn't Canadians representing Canadian financial interests participate in the direction and in the administration of Canadian business that they could finance? They cannot do it now; it is impossible.
We want a modern, up-to-date financial system, not one that copes only with the conditions that apply today but with conditions ten years in the future and lays the framework for the next 25 years. That is what we need, not something that looks back at the model "T". You do not build a modern car by looking at a 1945 model. Unfortunately, that is what is being done with the Bank Act. We have to do a lot of rethinking with regard to this.
There is going to be a report by the commission on corporate concentration. I will be very interested in that document. It may show some ways of doing away with difficulties in the structures of banks at present. There are not enough directors representing ordinary shareholders.
I wish to mention a few other matters with regard to banks. I would like to see a reduction in the value and quantity of the qualifying shares of directors. It should not be necessary that you be a director of Power Corporation, Massey Ferguson, Sun Life or any other major company in order of qualify for a bank directorship. They should sort of democratize.
Qualifying shares of some banks today cost as high as $50,000 or $60,000. If the bank wants you as a director and you have empty pockets, they will lend you the $50,000 or $60,000 to buy the qualifying shares. That is wrong. Such a director will be beholden to the administration of the bank. There is a very great danger that that individual will be beholden to the administration and really be a tame director. That is not necessary and should not be there.
There are many other changes we would like to see. I will not go into them in detail. They call for getting on with the changes to the Bank Act. The parliamentary secretary said "at some time in the future", "as soon as possible". That leaves us in a very unsatisfactory position. It is not because parliamen-

January 23, 1978
Bank Act
tary business is being upset or that it is going to come on in an election year. I am almost prepared to bet some of our good currency that, depending upon the date of the election, it could be that we will be back before this House asking for a further extension. I do not see any activity on the bill prior to June. If the election is not in June but in October or November, then along comes the introduction of the Bank Act and first reading. Second reading will take some time.
I have already shown what the waltz steps are with regard to the public hearings. Therefore, March 31, 1979, will be long past history before the bill is passed and time is given to the banks to get into position. There will have to be a further extension. As one says, that is a hell of a way to run the store.
This goes right back to the former Minister of Finance, Mr. Turner. He missed the boat in 1973 by either failing to persuade the administration or not coming to the decision to have a royal commission, on the style of the Porter commission, laying out in clear terms the requirements of the Canadian financial system for the next generation, seeing what dramatic change there has been in the past 20 years. If that had been done, we would not be talking about this bill today. We would have a new Bank Act in position.
As a final point, the Inspector General of Banks should not play such a passive role. His is a role of merely receiving reports and seeing that certain things qualify under the guidelines and regulations. It is not an initiative on his part to examine as far as I would like. We had the operations of one of the banks that was carrying on here for a while. The public was saved from any disaster by reason of the fact that the other banks arranged that one of them would purchase the business. That is not good enough. The Inspector General of Banks must have more investigative powers than that.
I foresee a much wider role for the Inspector General in that an awful lot more institutions would have to qualify under the Bank Act. If they are carrying on the business of banking, they will have to pay their dues. There is no such thing as a free ride. If people want to carry on the business of banking, let them or their organization comply with the regulations that are designed, not necessarily to protect the competition but to protect the public. It is on that basis that I and my colleagues are very critical of the government with regard to the timing and casual approach to it. Therefore it is conceivable that later this day we will express our displeasure in another way.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government's decision to postpone again revision of the Bank Act is a sure sign to the Canadian people of the inefficient way the country is being administered by this cabinet and this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
The government has experienced for the past five years, not to mention the past ten years this Prime Minister has been in power, a tremendous growth in the civil service. Here, in the national capital region, there has been a dramatic increase in highly paid civil servants in the Prime Minister's office, the Finance Department, and in the Bank of Canada.

Despite the fact that the Bank Act was supposed to be revised in 1977, the government is now requesting another delay. It will be 1979 before we get around to the so-called decennial revision that was supposed to be done in 1977.
Inflation and unemployment in this country, coupled with the flip-flop by the Prime Minister on wage and price controls, long ago convinced many Canadians that, despite the problem of national unity, this government does not know where it is going with the economy.
The uncertainty and the drift which are apparent at the present time, and which have been building for some time in the business sector of the economy, are being added to by such things as the inability of the government to revise the Bank Act on schedule.
The Bryce Commission on Corporate Ownership is, I understand, almost completely ignoring the extent of financial concentration which finds expression in the chartered banks. As parliamentarians we should be concerned about the expression used by Allan Fotheringham in the January 23 issue of Macleans to the effect that Canada "is controlled not by politicians but by a system of interlocking directorships, with the banks as the lynch-pin." This statement seems scarcely exaggerated in the light of recent economic events. We have seen, for instance, Inco shifting certain of its operations to Guatemala and Indonesia at the cost of thousands of Canadian jobs; we have learned of other multi-national corporations deciding to move parts of their operations to countries abroad with a corresponding loss of employment here. Unfortunately, such actions are not discouraged by a government which, far from protesting, supports the corporations lavishly by offering them all kinds of fiscal loopholes and tax breaks, including tax deferrals.
The present over-concentrated and semi-monopolistic banking system is a further factor in encouraging corporate policies of a kind which have been criticized so severely in this House in recent months.
Like so many other big businesses in this country, the banks did not relish the basic premise of the Carter commission that "a buck is a buck from whatever source it comes," though they do not hesitate to act on this premise when dealing with the large non-financial corporations.
Dr. John Porter in his book "The Vertical Mosaic" written,
I think it was, in 1966, showed how 907 men in Canada shared 81 per cent of the directorships of the dominant corporations as well as 58 per cent of the bank directorships and a similar proportion of the directorships of the life insurance companies, Mr. Fotheringham, in the article to which I have referred, points out that today the extent of this concentration has become even more pronounced; no more than 300 men centred on the boards of the banks, hold more than 3,000 directorships of corporations with total assets of $700 billion. I may say I am not sure as to the correctness of that latter figure. My information is that nine of the 12 chartered banks in Canada had total assets amounting to $247.4 billion in 1977, up by 21

per cent from the year earlier, with each of the five leading banks increasing its assets-$17.9 billion in the case of the Toronto-Dominion and $23.1 billion in the case of the Bank of Nova Scotia. However, it seems to me Mr. Fotheringham is perfectly accurate in his other statistics.
I suggest the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) should inform himself on what the Norwegian government has done recently to democratize the banking system in that country because its measures serve as a good example, one which we might well follow instead of allowing the economy to be increasingly controlled by the banks and by the large corporations.
At a time when the whole world is seriously concerned about the operations of the OPEC oil cartel and with the possibility of the existence of a uranium cartel-indeed the Prime Minister has suggested that such a cartel might be used effectively in the nickel industry-it is not surprising that the decennial revision of the Bank Act is being continually postponed by a government which does not wish to interfere too greatly with the cozy cartel of Canadian bankers who, in co-operation with the Bank of Canada, have a monopoly on producing money.
The Prime Minister has referred to the bankers publicly as "the worst bitchers of all in the Canadian economy" and has expressed himself as being ashamed of the profits the banks have been making-some $232 million in 1977. Such being the case one might expect that the right hon. gentleman would want to do something about these "bitchers" with the big profits. But such is not the case. What we, as representatives of the people, get, is a request from him and from the government to postpone revision of the Bank Act further.
Let us briefly review bank profits for the year ended October 31, 1977. First, the Figures for total revenue. The Royal Bank showed a percentage increase of 12.3, the Bank of Commerce an increase of 11 per cent, the Bank of Montreal an increase of 11.1 per cent, the Bank of Nova Scotia an increase of 13.3 per cent, and the Toronto-Dominion Bank an increase of 10.8 per cent. This, Mr. Speaker, is at a time when the non-financial corporate sector is on its proverbial you-know-what and when the government is spending $1.5 billion trying to get the rest of the private sector moving.
Let us turn, now, to after-tax profits. Between 1976 and 1977 the Royal Bank saw an increase from $157.4 million to $168.8 million. Profits of the Bank of Commerce rose from $145 million to $150 million-I am rounding these figures out, now. In respect of the Bank of Montreal, they went from $95 million to $122 million; for the Bank of Nova Scotia they went from $116 million to $131 million, and for the Toronto-Dominion Bank they went from $92 million to $100 million. That represents the increase in net earnings of these shares for these large corporations.
One of the reasons the government is not anxious to revise the system and get greater control is the fact that the net earnings per share of the Royal Bank went from $4.30 to $4.61 between 1976 and 1977; in relation to the Bank of Commerce
Bank Act
they went from $4.19 to $4.32; for the Bank of Montreal they increased from $2.71 to $3.18; for the Bank of Nova Scotia they went from $2.83 to $3.19, and for the Toronto-Dominion Bank they increased from $2.43 to $2.63. That represents pretty darn good profit in light of the remainder of the economy, and shows again the coddling that has gone on and the special protection of power that has been given to these five large banks, along with the central bank, to control the money supply in a semi-monopolistic if not entirely monopolistic system.
Of course we were not surprised to hear from the representatives of these large corporations, that is, the Canadian Bankers' Association, that the white paper produced by the government followed closely the recommendations of that association. Nor were we surprised to see the stock market shares of the five chartered banks with the largest assets rise to the biggest gain in over two years.
There are really only 12 banks in Canada, and among these, the five I mentioned, since they control 90 per cent of all banking assets, are in effect, if not in a theoretical monopoly position, in a semi-monopolistic position, and in respect of many functions are in a monopolistic position because of their role in the open market operations of the Central Bank of Canada in increasing or decreasing the money supply of this nation.
These banks have historically managed to keep unions at arm's length, even though they control 60 per cent of all consumer lending in this country, by being allowed by the government here in Ottawa to have these so-called banker s hours.
These large banks have ostensibly favoured women for their staff positions such as tellers, etc., where they constitute some 70 per cent of the labour force in the banking industry, but they make sure that only 2 per cent of them ever get management positions. British Columbia has special problems. I will go back a few years to the time of the NDP government there. It took them a long time but they seem to have realized the wisdom of most of the legislation that they said was so bad during the last provincial election.
One piece of legislation dealt with a vital and importnat issue-it is the "seize or sue" legislation which provides that you do not get two kicks at a debtor. For instance, if you want to seize his car, you can do so, sell it, and thus satisfy the debt. But you are not allowed to seize the car and then sue for the deficiency. That adds insult to injury. The interest rate on the original debt is high enough to cover the risk of loss. The legislation also provided that the goods could not be seized if only one-third of the debt remained; in that case, you had to go after the debt itself.
That is pretty sensible legislation and the present administration in British Columbia has accepted it. Surprisingly, the banks of British Columbia do not accept it and have consistently refused to comply with the law. The courts of British Columbia have told the banks that they are wrong and that the province has jurisdiction in this area. In effect, it has told them that if they are going to lend money on a car or take a chattel mortgage, they must comply with the law of the province.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: MEASURE TO EXEMPT INTEREST ON MUNICIPAL BONDS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act to exempt the interest of municipal bonds from income tax.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion is appearing in my name for the second time, and the reason for unanimous consent to proceed with it this afternoon is that I did allow it to stand a couple of times in favour of other members who had more pressing matters.
It is unfortunate that private members' hour does not really allow for debate because many of the comments made last time this was introduced, on May 24, 1977, could have been better answered then rather than now. However, as you know, time does not permit. As a consequence I am now bringing this motion forward and I intend to press the motion again and again if necessary until I have some form of support for it.
I am going to deal with the comments that were made when the matter was brought up last year and I intend to add some new arguments. When the matter was brought up last time, the New Democratic Party made an intervention in the afternoon and they actually made mention of three points. First of all they suggested my motion would benefit only the rich. I know that the New Democratic Party have a thing about people being wealthy; however, I think this is nonsense. I started out in municipal life as a councillor for Sidney over 21 years ago and in those days we sold our municipal debentures over the counter to farmers in the area, and they certainly were not wealthy. The New Democratic Party also pointed out that the motion would distort the tax system. The tax system, Mr. Speaker, is so badly distorted as we have seen by the bill this afternoon, the bills in this session so far, and the bills we expect to have, that my suggestion could only serve to clarify it rather than destroy it. Lastly the NDP suggested this would create a tax haven, as in the United States, because the debentures would qualify for deductions. Of course, Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what I am trying to do, provide a tax haven. In the suggestions which I will make later, I will be able to deal with it in more detail.
The Liberal party intervened also last May 24 and they brought up a number of points which I thought were very interesting. Their first point was that the government had no business changing laws to finance municipal governments. The Department of Urban Affairs was set up to do that exactly, to intervene and meddle in urban affairs. In fact, the municipalities are creatures of the provinces. We know that, their activities are governed by the provinces. But there is nothing to say that when the federal government is given an opportunity at no cost to itself to reduce the tax burden on municipalities and their people, that it should not do just that.
The Liberal party mentioned at that time that it was up to the provincial governments to give city governments more taxing powers. This is the very reason that I wish we could have debated the matter at that point. Frankly my dander was

up at that point, and my anger at the nonsensical way in which the arguments were presented would have made for a good debate. It is absolute, utter nonsense to think that the municipal governments could have more taxing powers of their own. They are taking from the people in the municipalities now the maximum amount of money through the realty taxes and there is no way more money could be expected from the taxpayers in that particular way. The provincial governments are powerless to change that situation given the restraints they have to face.
The Liberal members suggested at that time that the proposal which I made would have an unfair impact because high income municipalities and individuals would benefit more than low income municipalities. If that is not identical to the socialist doctrine put forward by the NDP I do not know what is. We expect that socialist doctrine from our friends to the left, but coming from across the way, it seems to me, shows the true nature of the Liberal party rather than a concerted effort to deal with the proposal put before them.
I was delighted to see that the Social Credit party at that point in time supported my motion. It is interesting to know that there are in the House of Commons at least two parties that have a free enterprise format in their policy. It is the only other party in the House obviously that is not a socialist party.
Mr. Speaker, having said that, I want to deal briefly with the fact that the voice of the municipalities in the province of Ontario, The Municipal World magazine, gave some space to my suggestion and they supported it. In doing so they asked for comments from the Minister of Urban Affairs, which I thought was a very good idea. The Minister of Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) did not then participate, as obviously he is not going to this afternoon because he is not in the chamber. However, the Minister of Urban Affairs did put forward some gobbledygook which was written in a bureaucratic type of language which I am confident the minister himself did not write. His argument, written up in the magazine, was that it would not necessarily offer benefits to the cities. Of course, it would offer benefits to the cities. That is the whole purpose of my motion.
The mail which I received from the various cities in Ontario, and at least one from outside Ontario, indicated that the aldermen in those cities thought that it would benefit them. The minister mentioned that because municipalities rely on foreign borrowing the effectiveness of the measure would be limited. Once again, Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the point I am trying to make. Because municipalities rely on foreign borrowing, this measure is needed. It is necessary. It would reduce the foreign borrowing of the municipalities and allow them to borrow in Canada with all the benefits going to Canadians.
Once you get through the few pages of double talk in the reply by the minister his final point was that it was unlikely it would enhance the Canadian balance of payments, position "in the short run". Of course it wouldn't enhance the balance of payments position in the short run. That is exactly the point I have been trying to make. In the short run there would be very little difference. But surely to goodness this government can

look for once beyond the short run. It could look beyond tomorrow. It could look a few years ahead and make some provision for municipalities and their problems as they continue to grow, so that ten years from now they will be in much better position. The debentures sold with ten, 15 or 20 year coupons will have to be honoured. Those that are being sold today will have to be honoured in ten, 15 or 20 years. It would take that long before this measure could really benefit the municipalities.
I am not going to take the full 20 minutes allotted to me. I want to deal with some points that I may not have fully covered the last time. It may add to my argument.
First, and most important, this is a means of assistance to the municipalities which will not require another costly self-perpetuating bureaucracy. The policy of this party has been clearly enunciated by our leader and others. We do not want to increase the bureaucracy. We have suggested that the controls be removed in a way which would reduce rather than increase the size of the civil service. The proposal I have put forward does not in any way add to the bureaucracy.
Second, unlike the comments by my friends to the left and their colleagues opposite, the small investor would receive a twofold benefit. First, his municipal taxes would be lowered. That was the main thrust of what I said when I presented the motion for the first time last year. The municipal taxes of all taxpayers in the cities, towns, villages and townships in Canada would be lowered. Second, in addition to the benefit of reduced taxes in the municipality, the income would not be subject to income tax. As I said, he would receive a twofold benefit.
More important, the municipalities would be able to finance their public debt from their own citizens. As I indicated a while ago, I started out in political life 21 years ago in Sidney. There we sold our debentures over the counter. If the municipal debentures are sufficiently attractive, there is no reason why they cannot be sold in that way.
I have a tremendous amount of faith in Canadian investors. I know that right now they have very little confidence in the economy of this country. Large amounts of money have been invested in the United States and other countries. I am quite happy to have this referred to as a tax haven. I am confident that given this relief from income tax on municipal debentures, the money will remain in Canada. They could be financed within the communities where the debentures are to be sold.
That would have a corollary benefit, that of adding to the relationship between the citizens and City Hall. They would get to know what is going on in their community much better than they do now. They would feel they are participating. It would make them better citizens and would lead to a better relationship.
I have a very strong feeling it would result in a diminishing of demand for funds in the foreign market. Last time I made the point that some $875 million went out of Canada in payments. Those dollars had to be borrowed in the first place.
Income Tax Act
The resultant diminution of borrowing on foreign markets might well bring down the interest rate even one quarter or one half point. Corporations that borrow abroad, as they necessarily do would be able to borrow at a lower interst rate. The decrease in inflationary pressure would benefit all sources rather than hinder them.
One of the main purposes of the proposed changes in the Income Tax Act would be to enable shareholders and small private companies to receive built up surpluses on a tax free or low tax basis. It would allow them to bring built up tax surpluses into circulation, helping to offset the depressed conditions in which we now find ourselves. This is one more way those tax surpluses could be put into circulation in Canada, making it attractive for people in the cities to invest in their own communities.
As I said before, a good deal of money goes outside Canada into tax havens. A competent professional service is required to enable them to do that. That cost is wasted. Making legal a tax haven for Canadians here at home without the attendant t high professional costs would meet the needs of all Canadians and lower interest costs attendant on proposed capital expenditures.
I have gone on longer than I intended. I want to bring out again the two major points of my original proposal. Reliance on foreign markets would be reduced and we would attract investors from Canada. My research indicates that the additional debt surplus would increase. In fact it has increased in recent years.
I was hopeful that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lumley) would take part in the debate this afternoon. He is a highly respected former municipal politician. He is well aware of the truth of what I am saying. He knows this measure would benefit the municipalities. Now that he has a good deal of clout in the Finance Department, I had hoped he might rise in his place and support this motion. However, we will have to wait and see what happens. I am not particularly hopeful. In the past the government has not been very receptive to suggestions that are sensible and which will help the ordinary individual.
I will leave it at this point, with the caution that if this motion is talked out this afternoon I will bring it back again and again until I get it through.

First, because they do it in the United States, the assumption is made that anything that is done in the United States must be better than anything that is done in Canada. Therefore, the idea keeps getting put forward for that reason. Second, it is put forward, and the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis) knows this as well as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lumley), because the need of

municipalities for funds is extreme. Their responsibilities far exceed the revenue base they have been given by the provincial governments which set them up. I argue that the need alone is no justification for making an amendment; as the hon. member himself indicated in his conclusion, it would be quite a tax rip-off. It would be a tax haven which he proceeded to justify. I do not think it can be justified. I will come to that in a moment.
Before I get to the substance, I want to reply to the two cheap shots the hon. member lowered himself to take during his remarks. In carefully listening to him, I noted only two cheap shots. The first crack was that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) was absent from the House right now. He suggested that indicated a lack of concern for municipalities. I hope the hon. member for Hastings was joking when he suggested the Minister of State for Urban Affairs ought to be here to listen to this old chestnut being kicked around again. I would much prefer to have the minister spend this hour doing the administrative side of his job, there being such a heavy demand upon his time.
The second cheap shot the hon. member for Hastings took was that directed toward the Liberal party.

speechtext: Shame!

He said that because we opposed a measure which so obviously favoured the rich, we were therefore socialists. The hon. member was drawing a far-fetched conclusion; there is a great deal of difference between being a socialist and simply wanting a fair tax system, which is the kind of system this party favours. It is simply a question of resisting the introduction into the system of benefits which would do far more for the rich than they would do for municipalities. That is the substantial point and it is one which the hon. member should recognize.
In the United States, where this rip-off has existed for many years, the savings to the rich in the form of income tax concessions have far exceeded the benefit of the lower interest rate which the municipalities are able to achieve by being in a position to offer tax-free bonds to those who buy them. A study recently carried out in the United States for President Carter showed that the loss in taxes to the federal treasury through this income tax privilege was far greater than the saving to the municipalities through lower interest payments. In other words, the municipalities and the whole system in the United States would be better served if municipal bonds were taxable, and if the federal government took the portion of tax which it collected on the interest accruing from municipal bonds and paid it over to the municipalities there would be far more money paid to the municipalities than is now the case through a measure which, in the end, is a tax haven, as the hon.

member himself concedes. The fact that it is done in the United States is not, in my opinion, sufficient to recommend the proposal-

This is the first time anyone who knows me has made such a charge against me. In fact, I am very pro-American and very close to the Americans. Nevertheless, I do not think we should copy their mistakes.
I suggest that in addition to it being a rip-off which benefits the rich more than it benefits the municipalities, the proposal of the hon. member for Hastings has the additional disadvantage of operating against free enterprise. I am sure the hon. member's constituents will be sorry to hear he is advocating tax proposals whose adoption would be damaging to free enterprise.
The hon. member, as we know, has been a municipal councillor and he is in a position to understand the need for easier access to capital. I suggest he has a responsibility to look beyond the needs of the municipalities, to stand back and consider the effect of the proposal he is making upon the economy as a whole. After all, his proposal is a far-reaching one and would involve hundreds of millions in lost revenue to the federal treasury, so he ought not to think of it as being simply an easy way by which the municipalities would get extra money. The changes suggested are such as to affect the balance between municipally conducted enterprises and those which operate in the free market.
I should like to quote, if I may, from the report of the Carter Commission on Taxation in which the commissioners rejected out of hand any proposal such as we are considering here. As recorded at page 125 of the fourth volume, the commissioners made this observation:
Where government undertakes activities which compete with those of private business, the exemption of government instrumentalities from tax to which their privately-owned competitors are subject provides the former with an advantage to which the latter may quite reasonably object. There are many examples of government-owned corporations which compete with privately-owned companies-
Municipalities presently contract out a great many of the activities for which the funds are provided by municipal taxpayers, for example, snow-shovelling, gardening, the cleaning of public buildings and, almost certainly, the construction of buildings which municipalities require. It is evident to me that if the tax benefit proposed were to be available to the municipalities, the balance would change and it would be cheaper for the taxpayers of a municipality through their councils to set up their own contracting companies, buy their own trucks and so on, and take on these jobs themselves because they could secure access to money at lower rates than the private sector.
It is true the municipal taxpayers would benefit-but only as municipal taxpayers. The country as a whole would be poorer because, as I have indicated, the benefit contemplated is one which would cost more than it would save. We would find municipalities putting up buildings and renting them to business, as is the case in the United States today; businessmen there putting up a building have to pay taxes at normal rates,

but municipalities can do it themselves a lot cheaper. If you go to the United States looking for a place to open a business, the first thing you find out is that municipalities are prepared to use this tax loophole for the benefit of individual companies. This is not the case in Canada because we have a fairer tax system.
I submit that in the broader perspective there is no advantage to the country in the type of proposal the hon. member recommends. Not only would it be of undue benefit to the rich but it would operate against the interest of free enterprise. I understand that a great many members on this side wish to speak on this proposal and I therefore am not willing to take up more time. Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to get back to the business of the House of Commons on its first day of the new session, although I am rather saddened by the fact that we are once again debating the somewhat ill-conceived and premature motion of the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis). My colleague, the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), has given an adequate position against the motion as outlined by the hon. member for Hastings. I should like to deal with some other ramifications of the motion should it ever be implemented by the government of Canada.
The exemption from income tax of the interest on municipal bonds has been proposed by the hon. member as a means of assisting local governments. The United States provides such an exemption, as my colleague has outlined. It provides this exemption from taxation of interest earned on both state and local bonds. With the exemption, investors would be willing to buy local bonds with rates lower than the rates on corporate or other government bonds. In this way the new tax advantages would be translated into reduced financing costs for the municipalities. The cost of the measure to the government is the forgone income tax revenue on local bond interest, and the benefit to the municipalities is the decreased interest rates.
I find this a very interesting proposal coming from a member of the Conservative party at this time of economic restraint. It appears from positions that have been made public by members of the Conservative party in the last few months that they are going to ride the big, over-spending government hobby-horse into the next election. However, along comes the hon. member for Hastings who proposes that the federal government should then forgo tax revenues in order to implement the kind of motion he has before us.

While the measure would undoubtedly have some success in achieving this result, there are significant defects which make the proposal undesirable for adoption in
