Canada. It is interesting to note that the interest exemption for state and local bonds in the United States has been widely criticized both within and outside the government. In fact, there have been numerous attempts by the administration to withdraw this exemption and replace it with a direct subsidy or some other form of financial aid which does not have the serious inequities and costly inefficiencies of the current interest exemption.
I know my colleague, the hon. member for Middlesex-Lon-don-Lambton (Mr. Condon), wishes to deal with a number of aspects of the motion. I should like to talk about the problems inherent in the proposal in respect of distribution of benefits by region. This proposed interest exemption is likely to have the opposite effect on local financing from the one it is intended to have, because this measure will benefit larger metropolitan centres more than smaller rural communities.
In making that statement I am fully cognizant of the problems faced by large municipalities since I am a member of parliament from metropolitan Toronto, and that metropolitan area has severe financial problems, whether they be in providing welfare, other social services and community services, or, in particular, transportation. I want to talk about transportation a little later on.
I am taking this position because I feel the hon. member has not really grasped the significance of implementing the motion or the impact this will have on large metropolitan areas to the detriment of smaller municipalities. I know by the constituency he represents that there are many, many small areas which I am sure would not want him to be misled into thinking this would benefit them when in fact it would benefit the large metropolitan areas.
Furthermore, it will help municipalities in the higher income provinces much more than the towns in lower income provinces. Surely this is a perverse effect, and such an outcome is not in the best interest of Canadian municipalities at large.
Municipalities and other local governments come under provincial jurisdiction. The role of the provincial and local levels of government varies greatly from province to province. Because of these regional differences there are substantial variations in the financial arrangements between these two levels of government. For example, there are wide variations in the provision and funding of health care. Provincial governments bear the major responsibility for health services, although municipalities may be delegated a considerable degree of authority. All ten provinces have exclusive responsibility for provincial health insurance, although financing is through premiums in Quebec, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia, and through general revenues in the remaining six provinces. For other health services, municipalities play varying roles. For example, in Newfoundland the municipalities make no financial contribution to hospitals or public health services. In other provinces, for example New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba, there are municipal hospitals with municipalities paying at least part of the capital cost of construction.

Differences exist among provinces as to the proportion of local funding for such services as education and also with regard to structure of local revenues. In Prince Edward Island, for example, the operational costs of education are competely financed by provincial grants to local school boards. Funds borrowed by school boards for the construction of schools are also guaranteed by the government in that province. By contrast, in Ontario local property taxes raise nearly half the total expenditures on education, with the balance financed by grants from the Ontario government.
On the revenue side, for example, the proportion of the funds raised through property taxation, debenture issues and other fees and taxes varies across the provinces. Such variations are reflected very clearly in the outstanding per capita municipal debt by province. I will not go into that, however, because I would be prolonging the debate.
When I spoke on this matter, I guess it was last year when the hon. member first brought it forward, I mentioned I felt it was premature because in the province of Ontario a government commission had been created and had reported. That was the Blair Commission headed by a former mayor of one of the municipalities which make up my constituency of York East in Toronto. That commission made certain recommendations to restructure municipal finances which are being studied by the Ontario government. The provincial treasurer says it bears further study, but he cannot accept some of the ramifications which would occur from an implementation of the Report of the Blair Commission. So the kind of proposal the hon. member is making really does not take into account work that is already being done in the province of Ontario in respect of municipal financing.
Therefore, I would like to make the point that we have to look at this proposal in the context of over-all Fiscal and constitutional reform. Last election we as a Liberal party made a number of promises in respect of aid to transportation. One of the arguments against that aid was that it was not within federal jurisdiction to interfere in assistance to municipalities, and perhaps it should be done in other ways, such as by making more revenues available to the provinces which in turn would make more revenues available to the municipalities. Perhaps that is, indeed, the solution. Perhaps we will have to say, as we have in respect of health care: Here are additional tax points; the provinces must raise the money and accept responsibility for giving money to the municipalities.
There is another side to that point, one I have been mentioning in speeches in my constituency at public gatherings, and it is that I believe the country is becoming too decentralized; that we are giving up too much fiscal and taxation power to the provinces. What is going to happen is that the rich provinces like Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia, in any further decentralized country, are going to become stronger; the poorer provinces, especially those in eastern Canada, are the ones which will suffer the most through decentralization or a diminution of powers. In any event, that follows from the arguments I have been making. I believe the motion proposed by the hon. member must be seen in the context of over-all

constitutional and fiscal reforms. We should not be dealing with it on a piecemeal basis, and for this reason I cannot support the motion.
One other aspect of the motion that bothers me is that it would encourage municipalities even more to raise funds without real recourse to a consideration of the problems that increased municipal expenditures might incur. Over the last few years everyone has been attacking the Government of Canada for not having tight reins on its purse, but provincial governments, municipal governments and provincial utilities have been some of the greatest masters of taxpayers' money.
During the last few years, provincial governments, municipal governments and provincial utilities such as Ontario and Quebec Hydro have gone outside the country in an attempt to raise money. Those utilities raised money in New York. In fact the premier of Ontario has been to Zurich, Geneva and other places in an attempt to raise money for provincial expenditures. The foreign borrowing which has been done by individual municipalities, utilities and provinces has distorted Canada's financial picture as well as the value of the dollar. Over the last few years the Canadian dollar was valued too high. Now we are experiencing a general correction in the value of the Canadian dollar. One of the principal causes for its overevaluation was the enormous provincial, municipal and utilities overseas borrowings.
I have been informed that the government of Canada does not owe a nickel outside of this country, that all of its public debt is raised through pension funds, through Canada savings bonds, and it is floated within the country. Therefore, the government knows what money is likely to be raised on the Canadian market. It does not go abroad to borrow money as the municipalities and provinces do.
Perhaps the hon. member should propose a constitutional amendment or an act of this House whereby the borrowings of municipalities, provincial governments and utilities should be subject to some over-all national financial plan or program.

In the Strathroy and Middlesex area, the provincial government is giving a 4.8 per cent increase in funds to the education system. Perhaps that is fine and it is within the guidelines, but

where was the provincial government when those 4,000-pupil schools were being built and millions of dollars in architectural fees were being paid out? Now the poor taxpayer has to pay for that. He is always the goat, especially in Ontario with its Conservative provincial government.
As was indicated by my colleague, this is a distortion in the financial decision-making process of local governments. The proposed interest exemption creates another serious bias in the capital market for privately issued bonds. If local governments increase their long term debt, either there must be an increase in over-all public-plus-private debt or else there must be a decrease in private debt. It is likely that municipalities will bid away at least some funds from the private sector, even if there is an increase in over-all debt as well. I wonder if this is what we want.
At the present time the backbone of this country is the small businessman. That has been the case for many years. As we have seen, small businesses have done very well in this country over the last 15 or 20 years. Why is that? It is because they are realistic enough to look down the road four or five years. Also, this government has helped and encouraged small businessmen in Canada to invest in the future.
I will not go too far on this, but I brought this to the attention of small businessmen in the Stratford-Middlesex-London-Lambton area. No government is perfect and every government can be criticized. My only criticism of this government with regard to small business is, as I have said on many occasions, that small businessmen are not getting a square deal out of banks. I think there are problems here and, as was mentioned by my friend, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), some time ago, banks do not look at small business as a potential for growing and developing, the potential for a bank to make more money out of business, which is the name of the game-free enterprise. At a time when the federal government is placing great importance on the economic contribution of the private sector, a move in the opposite direction is obviously undesirable, as I just mentioned.
Moreover, it is likely that the smaller corporations would be hurt most by this measure, and we do not want that with the economy in a questionable state at present and with the government doing as much as it can to revitalize Canadian industry and business. The people we want to take care of first are the small businessmen who need extra capital advance. That extra one or two men in a small plant are the backbone of our country.
Some people will say that big business is the only way to go, as my friend, the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis), has said. He wants to get into big business and to give opportunities to people who have tax havens and advantages. I disagree with that. I am critical of this government so far as banking for small business is concerned.
The income tax exemption would be of no use to tax-exempt institutions, such as pension funds, and unattractive to inves-

Income Tax Act
tors with low marginal tax rates, such as pensioners with low incomes. Where will the money come from for the people who should be given this opportunity? This government has proven time and time again that when they consider the interests of the people, they consider people in all segments of society, not only special tax-exempt classes. The proposed exemption thus also creates a distortion in the type of investor to which municipal bonds are attractive.
The proposed exemption creates a bias in the decision-making process of investors. The tax-exempt status of municipal bonds would be most attractive to investors, both corporate and individual, with the highest marginal tax rates, and not attractive at all to tax-exempt or low tax investors. That, after all, is what this country was built on. This government looks at all the people, not only at certain people to whom it gives special benefits. I do not believe that we should set apart different classes, something which we on this side have not done in the past.
Now I should like to say a few words about subsidies to high income taxpayers. Investors with high marginal tax rates would be willing to buy tax-exempt local bonds as compared to regular bonds so long as their after tax position was no worse with the tax-exempt bonds. If all the tax-exempt securities were purchased by individual taxpayers with the highest combined federal and provincial rates in excess of 60 per cent, then in theory the interest rate required to attract these purchasers would only need to be slightly less than 40 per cent of rates on other comparable bonds.
In this circumstance, the full benefit of the subsidy would be reaped by municipal governments in the form of reduced financing costs. This would occur because the investors would be in about the same after tax position whether they purchased regular, taxable bonds or tax-exempt bonds. The benefit to investors in the form of the tax exemption would be only enough to offset the tax that would have been due on a taxable bond. For the various levels of government, the reduced interest payments by municipal governments would be equal to the revenue lost by the federal and provincial governments. This is the mechanism of tax-free municipal bonds, in theory.
What we are saying on this to the people is: "Yes, this is a great idea, you won't have any problems. It is beautiful for you, the individual, but in the long run the federal and municipal governments will pick up the tab". If we are going to give something to someone, let us give to him and leave it with him, not take it back with the other hand.
In practice, however, municipalities are unlikely to experience a reduction in interest rates of anywhere near the 40 per cent implied by the top marginal tax rates. Approximately half of municipal debentures are currently held by pension funds, foreign investors, other municipalities and other provinces, none of which is taxable. If the interest rates on municipal debentures were to fall significantly, these institutions would no longer find it desirable to hold the debt. As they left the market it would be impossible to sell all the debt to individual taxpayers in the highest marginal tax bracket, and certainly they would not accept it. They would say: "It is good now, but
[Mr. Condon.l
what about the future? You will take it all back from me anyway, so that does not make sense". If you give something to people, make sure they have it in their pockets; do not take it away with the other hand. As a result, significant portions would need to be sold to lower income individuals with lower tax rates and to corporations with combined federal and provincial rates of 46 per cent to 51 per cent. Who in God's name in a low tax bracket can afford to put out money for this? They do not do so anyway so they cannot have any benefit from it. The ones who should be receiving the break are not getting it; and the ones who should not be receiving it are receiving it. So the rich get richer and the poor get poorer.
I can tell you that that is not the Liberal philosophy. This government's philosophy is that we should share. We have done this in the past and we will do it again.

speechtext: At five o'clock the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) had the floor, and he has 31 minutes left.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate your warning hon. members as to how much time I have, but I must say that one is tempted to try to use that time, and I do not think that should be the response of a responsible member of parliament.
At five o'clock I was dealing with the capacity of banks to support small business in Canada. The record of banking institutions supporting and encouraging the growth of small business in Canada is one of the poorest in the western world. We pointed out this afternoon that there are 15,000 separately chartered banks in the United States. In Canada there are 12; probably only six of them are effective in terms of size. A non-aggressive and non-imaginative banking system like ours, which does not go out and seek to help entrepreneurs get small Canadian businesses underway, makes a major contribution to the economic malaise in which we now find ourselves.
I can give an example of this. A small entrepreneur who wants to set up a small hamburger stand will get short shrift from any of the major banks in Canada unless he has a fantastic amount of collateral or guarantees or unless he puts his house, his car and everything he has on the line. However, if instead of going the independent route he decides to associate himself with the McDonald's hamburger chain, the money will start flowing out of the conventional lending institutions of Canada, particularly banks, like you wouldn't believe. The result is that people like McDonald's-and I do not particularly have anything against them as they probably make a very good hamburger-

speechtext: "They do it all for you".

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext:
I will tell you who they do not do it for-the small competitive Canadian businessman who does not have the same opportunity to do that kind of massive advertising and use their techniques of merchandising. Their product is market tested in the most successful market in the world, the United States, before it is offered in this country. We had better understand that the small businessman in Canada must have the same kind of help from our financial institutions as they get. He is not getting it at the present time. Anyone who
Bank Act
has McDonald's backing can go to any bank in Canada and find that the response is "Away you go if you are associated with the clowns".
They had a wonderful promotion technique in the lower mainland of British Columbia. They invited all the politicians to take a day at a McDonald's hamburger stand and sell hamburgers, with all the profits to go to a worth-while charity. It was worth-while too, as I believe it was for crippled children or some such organization. I told them I would not go. I said that if they wanted to contribute to charity they should go right ahead without sucking in all the political people in the community to promote their hamburgers. I said I would sell hamburgers if the profits were to go to the small businessmen that McDonald's have driven to the wall in my community.
We have to look carefully at the way the lending institutions in Canada are driving small independent businesses to the wall. This all comes back to the way we organize and control the financial institutions in Canada. Unless we start to do something for the entrepreneurs of Canada we will not be able to buy a Canadian hamburger. It will be breakfast at "Denny's" and supper at "McDonald's." There will be franchises from one end of the country to the other and I do not want to see that. I want Canadian independence and I want a uniqueness in our services. All we are getting at the moment is that market tested formula from southern California and New York state. It is impossible for Canadian entrepreneurs to compete without the kind of training, the kind of leadership and the kind of financial assistance from our institutions that they have been crying for and have not been receiving from this government and particularly from the banks of Canada.
We all like to stand in this House and say we are in favour of small business, but little has been done to help small business. Some very specific areas could be tackled. The government could have taken these steps instead of trying to delay changes to the Bank Act for another year, had it had the courage to grasp the nettle. One of the problems with this government is that perhaps the minister would have been kicked out for doing that, as the former minister was; then we would have to start again from square one with a new minister.
I have always heard about the banking lobby, Mr. Speaker. As a member of parliament I have been lobbied from mining, from forestry and from fishing interests, but I have never had a banking lobby in my office. I could not figure out why until I realized that there are so many people in the place next door who hold directorships in banks that there is no point in their coming to an ordinary member of parliament. The conflict of interest in the place next door as it relates to the appointment of members of the Senate to directorships on the boards of the major banks of Canada. And the question of whether that has influenced the legislation presented to this House, should be looked at very carefully.
We had a tough year in 1977. Labour was held down. They attempted to hold wage increases at six per cent, and they are not too much higher than that with inflation at 9.5 per cent. But what happened to the banks in that terrible year? The dear old Royal Bank, the largest, managed to increase its

Bank Act
revenue from $2.44 billion to $2.74 billion, a 12.3 per cent increase in profit in one year. That is well ahead of any wage settlement I saw and well ahead of the majority of profit-taking in other sectors of the Canadian economy.
Banks in this country are given very special privileges. The revenues of the Bank of Nova Scotia increased from $1.5 billion to $1.7 billion last year, or 13.3 per cent. And so it goes with all the banks. They look more out of the economy last year than they deserved. What is the government doing about it? It is delaying changes to the Bank Act.
If there is one thing we should be doing in this House it is to change the way we regulate banking in Canada. Unless we can make the banking system competitive we should think about having a public banking system. It must be one or the other. We cannot continue with what we have now, which is the worst of both worlds in terms of funding and financing the business of this country and creating employment. It is the small businessman who provides most of the employment. His is a labour-intensive business; he needs help. He is not into the area of massive technology and of attempting to eliminate his workers because of the capitalization in his industry. If we are ever to have increased employment it will be in the servicing sector and the small business sector. This is the area we should be encouraging if we are to reduce unemployment.
We get no answers whatsoever from this government when we ask about bringing forward banking legislation which would regulate competition and would require banks to offer small loans and increase the amount of those small loans. Even under the Small Businesses Loans Act you are limited to $75,000. Anyone who has had experience with small business knows that you cannot do much with $75,000, yet loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act are still limited to $75,000-if you can get money under it. In most cases the money is simply not available. There is no legislative requirement on a bank to lend money under its low interest provisions. That is where we should have begun in terms of legislation to help small business and in terms of regulating and controlling banks in order to provide for loans of higher amounts at low interest for small business. I want to see the situation where when a businessman comes to a town there are four banks competing to finance him. The way it is now, you almost have to break down the bank manager's door to get in to say hello! And then he is so fat and sassy that he could not care less, because he is making money by lending to conventional large borrowers or playing games with the American franchise houses all across Canada. The banks of this country had better get interested or they will find changes that will be untenable to them from an operational point of view. They have not performed the service of creating employment in this country, and their record of massive profits in the last two years and little help to small business is a prime example of their neglect in this area.
This government should move toward providing special training for entrepreneurs. I should like to see this done in a private way. We face heavy competition from American entrepreneurs partly because of their larger markets, partly because of the larger variety available to them, and partly because of
the greater number of people available to market test products. We have the problem of isolated pockets of population. There is the lower mainland and the Toronto-Montreal complex, but generally it is very difficult to market test a product in Canada compared to the United States, which has such huge market testing areas as New York city with ten million people. We have not given enough consideration to the question of solving this problem but one way would be through a special training program for Canadian entrepreneurs. This program could be offered through the universities or technical schools. We cannot create more employment without giving our small entrepreneurs some help.
West Germany, Japan and many other countries in the western world have set up trading companies. Their purpose is to make contact with overseas businessmen, arrange contracts and then to allow local small business to fill those contracts.
Our own Export Development Corporation, which should be active in this area, unfortunately continues to favour major colossal business over small business. The result is again that the larger businesses, which tend to be foreign owned and foreign controlled, receive by far the most help from the EDC.
In terms of government spending, what we need to do is to allocate a guaranteed portion of that spending to small business so we can allow those entrepreneurs to grow and get into competition with those at the larger business level. This has been done successfully in the United States. They have decentralized their purchasing into areas of need, but again they have decreed that those products should be produced by small business.
We must consider removing the sales tax which is extremely regressive, not only from the point of view of the purchaser but also from the point of view of the small businessman. He cannot continue having to tack this on to his product and expect to have success. Because he is the last genuinely competitive part of our economy, we are handicapping him more and more.
I do not believe for a moment that the various sectors of this economy are in any way competitive with each other. I believe, as most people do, that prices are administered, but they are not at that lower level. Ask the small clothier what kind of competition there is between him and The Bay, Woodward's or Eaton's. They can buy their products at massive discount prices. The small entrepreneur is stuck with buying them at a higher price and he has to give superlative service in order to compete with mass merchandising techniques.
We need, of course, low and middle income tax cuts. We need the employment tax credit that has come up and been suggested in this House many times. But what we need most of all, and this is really where I began these remarks, is an industrial strategy. An essential and vital part of that strategy is change in the financial institutions of Canada to make them competitive, change to make them effective and to put money where it is socially desirable. In Canada today, if you are not talking about creating public employment, the small,
