independently owned Canadian business is where loans should go. That is not happening. We have not had an industrial strategy. The failure of this government to process banking changes now rather than the old delay, delay, delay gives the Canadian people, certainly my constitutuents, no reason whatsoever to have any confidence that this government understands anything about improving the economy and solving the massive unemployment that we face.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government has always prided itself on bringing forward progressive legislation. This is the supreme example of their progressive legislation-progressing the bill forward one year because they do not have the legislation ready.
I remember just a few weeks ago when we were debating the income tax bill the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) sat here and harangued the opposition time and again because we were slowing down debate, because we were slowing down legislation when there was so much the government wanted to do. We were impeding all that progress which they had in mind. That was in the middle of December.
One would think with that kind of comment coming from the Minister of Finance that they had a series of bills ready to go and that as soon as we were past that income tax bill there would be another measure ready to work on. Here is a bill that is overdue a year or more. It is not only overdue in terms of the government calendar-because the white paper came out approximately twelve months ago-but it is overdue as well in terms of the needs of the country. Yet the government is sitting on its hands. I suppose the reason might be that some of the members of the banking committee of the other place, which the member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) has talked about, have been running scared of the attitudes toward this legislation and they want it stopped for as long as possible. At any rate, they are not ready to progress as they ought to be. I can imagine that a week or two from now we are going to hear howls from the various ministers saying that we are slowing down legislation.
I know the banks in Canada have enjoyed a reputation for being strong financial institutions. I think they have prided themselves on the fact that during the great depression in the 1930s there was not one bank in Canada that went belly-up. That provides security for the money lenders in Canada. I remember also that while the banks remained very secure during the 1930s, the farmers did not, and the small businessmen did not. There were all kinds of foreclosures all across Saskatchewan where we were living at that time. There were people just walking away from their farms, leaving them and allowing the banks to inherit them. An uncle of mine who had a good farm in central Saskatchewan with excellent farm buildings and a fairly new house sold his whole farming operation for $1 in 1939 and let someone else take over the mortgage. The banks did fairly well in the 1930s and did not feel too much pain.
Whilst we do need that kind of security and stability in our country, we also need some competition in the money market. I took my university undergraduate and graduate training in
Bank Act
the United States, and spending seven years in the United States allowed me to look a little bit at the way the lending institutions operate in that country. In the 1930s we in Canada looked with pride at our record compared to the number of bank failures in the United States. You could drive down some of the streets in Chicago and see some of the old bank buildings that were used as banks previously and then folded in 1933 because Mr. Roosevelt closed them. Their security was not very good. In the 1930s they corrected that; they provided insurance for their depositors. What we need is a system similar to the kind they have in the United States.
I spoke to an attorney in Washington, D.C. this afternoon. He specializes in banking and he told me that in the United States there are 14,000 banks; 6,000 national banks, which would be similar to our banks here in Canada, and 8,000 state banks. The national banks have approximately 60 per cent of the assets in the United States, and the state banks have the other 40 per cent, in addition to the savings and loans associations that are scattered all across the United States. If you go to any bank in any city in any state, you find there is some competition.
One of my constituents is building a small chain of retail outlets. They are not very grandiose. They serve the public very well. He is an aggressive salesman. He is trying to establish a new business. He is providing entrepreneurial leadership to some people who want to invest. He is providing employment that was not there before.
When this constituent wants to open a new store, even though he has a record of success he has to go to the bank and prove to that banker that he does not need the money before he has enough security to open another branch. He has to prove that he does not need the money before he can get it.
He decided to open another branch in the city of Bellingham. As soon as he walked across the border, he had two or three banks begging him for the business. I say to myself, what is going on? Here is a fellow, unknown in the state of Washington, who the banks want to serve. They are competing for the opportunity to serve him. However, in British Columbia they look the other way. They thumb their nose at him.
Something is wrong with our system when our Canadian institutions do not want to help Canadian entrepreneurs, when the same Canadian entrepreneurs can go to the United States and get money at just about any lending institution they walk into. Not only that, they can get the money at about 50 per cent less cost than here in Canada. In Canada they must pay 12 per cent or 13 per cent for their line of credit while there they can pick it up at 8 per cent. No wonder business is leaving Canada and going to the United States.
If one of this government's sins has been control of the money supply by printing too much of it, the other one has been allowing the institutions to be so tight-fisted in their policies that they have controlled the money supply in that

January 23, 1978
Bank Act
way. They have not allowed an equal distribution across the country of opportunity in entrepreneurial business.
Looking again at the system in the United States, you can go into a city bank or a state bank and you know that that private institution is indigenous to that particular area. You can rest assured that the president, chairman and directors of the board of that bank are from that community. They all live there and have their roots there. They want business to succeed in that community. They approach the businessman from an entirely different perspective from the banker here in Canada.
A lot of local bank managers would love to do something for the local businessman, but their hands are tied. The local bank manager has a limit of $50,000 he can lend the businessman. If the required loan is more than that, he must get approval from the district office. If the amount is too large, it goes from the district office to the head office. Where is the head office located? It happens to be in Toronto. They really care about White Rock, Langley or Cloverdale, don't they? Where are they? They could not care less about the prosperity of that particular community they are supposed to be serving.
A bank manager lives in a community. He has his roots there. He would love to do something for a businessman but he cannot because his head office stops him. In addition, often the manager is rotated from one place to another. By the time he barely gets his roots into one community, he is transferred to another branch in another community. He may never get his roots down the way he would like.
This government, with great temerity, is recognizing that the economic base is shifting from what has traditionally been central Canada and is moving westward. The other day the mayor of Winnipeg said that the financial base was moving to Winnipeg. That is the geographic centre of Canada. Certainly the economic base is gravitating toward Alberta and British Columbia. Maybe it is time we had some revisions to the Bank Act that allowed regional interests to express themselves in the financial community.
About ten years ago the then premier of British Columbia, W. A. C. Bennett, came forward with a budget and made a speech in the legislature of British Columbia. He proposed a Bank of British Columbia. I still remember the guffaws and shouts of horror across Canada that the premier of British Columbia would have the temerity to suggest that we ought to have a Bank of British Columbia. It was as though that was some kind of financial heresy. What is wrong with having a Bank of British Columbia that is uniquely British Columbian, that sees as its responsibility the growth of British Columbia, that is sensitive to the needs of that community, that draws on the resources of the people in that community and draws all its personnel from the community to man that bank? What is wrong with that?
It still strikes me with some kind of surprise the chagrin he had to face from the financial community across Canada for even suggesting there ought to be a local bank in British Columbia. By the time that idea got combed through the
[Mr. Friesen.J
financial brains of central Canada, it was thoroughly diluted. However, that is the direction we will have to go.
We must come to grips with the need for regional expression of the financial needs of the people in a banking organization, and the investment of the funds of that banking organization to meet the needs of that community. We can no longer afford the days when a farmer, who is a small businessman, walks into a bank and borrows money for the intervening months until his crop comes in, leaving that bank thinking that the bank manager has done him a favour, while he pays 13 per cent interest on the note. The bank is operating a service for these people.
If we want to stimulate our economy and stimulate small business in our country, we must look upon the small businessman as a friend, not as a potential liability. With 60 per cent of the work force in this country employed in small business, we have to realize that these people are the backbone of our country and that they have to be served.
This government's idea of progressive legislation is to postpone for one year legislation we ought to be dealing with today. That is its idea of progressiveness. I say shame for being so slow in keeping its legislative program going that we cannot even deal with issues that ought to be dealt with today to make sure that we have a healthy and thriving economy. It is time we got this legislation moving, so that the people across Canada who are most affected by this restrictive legislation can get the service they deserve and we can get the people of this country working in the way they want to be working.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this measure to extend the Bank Act; the request for extended time in which to consider the revision of the Bank Act is an indication of the government's lack of ability and its failure to deal successfully with the economic situation. We are obviously facing an unsettling and uncertain period economically, and while not all the problems are domestic in origin, a great many of them have certainly been caused by the ineptitude of hon. gentlemen opposite and by the failure of the administration to deal with the financial woes of the country.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is rarely in the House these days. He goes about the country like an optimistic choirboy telling people how the country is going to grow. But how can it grow when our principal trading partners, the United States, Western Europe and Japan, are all reporting a low level of activity and show little possibility of doing better in the coming year? Surely the minister's statements must be taken with a considerable measure of salt. The outlook for the United States continues to be far from cheerful, only a low level of economic activity being predicted.
Revision of the Bank Act is long overdue. Parliament has to deal with the problems presented by the so-called near-banks, and a situation in which Canadian banks feel they are handicapped when competing with foreign-based banks because of the way in which the regulations presently operate. Then there
January 23, 1978

are a number of internal banking issues; for example, what should be done about the rapid increase in the financial muscle of the credit unions. The success of the unions is to be applauded, but it makes sense that the regulations and restrictions affecting financial institutions should be of a reasonable nature and applied with reasonable fairness to all.
While the government delays legislation to revise the Bank Act, Canadian banks are going ahead with participation in leasing and factoring, which means managing companies for a fee. The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and the Banque Provinciale du Canada have established wholly-owned leasing subsidiaries, and the Royal Bank of Canada has close to 100 per cent interest in an established leasing company. In banking circles it was felt the revised act would allow the banks to become direct participants in leasing and factoring. It would seem Ottawa has already given tacit approval to the banks to engage in these activities.
This is not a good situation. It might well be an advantage to the economy that banks should become involved in leasing and factoring, but as the law presently stands they may not engage in such activities though they may invest in a portion of the equity of such companies. If the government intends to allow leasing and factoring on the part of the banks, the whole question should be discussed in this chamber as soon as possible. If the banks have received some sort of assurance from the government that their activities in connection with leasing and factoring will be legitimized within a few years, we should know about it. A tacit understanding that legislation will eventually be changed to suit the needs of the banks seems to be both unwise and undemocratic. If parliament is to exercise any influence upon what is to happen, it is time the legislation was brought forward.
That the government has already acquiesced in the situation appears to be substantiated by the fact that the Inspector-General, Mr. William Kennett, has already given permission for several banks to assume 100 per cent ownership of leasing and factoring establishment. If the new Bank Act does not permit leasing or factoring there will certainly be major financial changes forthcoming. All the banks are watching to see whether complete ownership of a leasing company allows better penetration of the market. In fact, there does not really seem to be much difference between leasing and factoring; this aspect of the situation will not be clarified for some time to come.
No discussion of the Bank Act would be complete without some general reference to the financial institutions of our country. The recent controversy as to whether Sun Life should move its head office out of Montreal has directed public attention upon our financial institutions. The Sun Life affair, against the background of other unsettling events in this country and abroad, has brought into question the strength and reliability of many of our financial institutions. We should not lose sight of the fact that Sun Life is the seventh largest corporation in Canada.
The question which has attracted such attention is whether or not a corporation has the right to move its offices and its
Bank Act
place of work in accordance with the best interests of its shareholders-the mutual policyholders, in the case of Sun Life. Western Canadians certainly applaud a move of the head offices of many of our institutions out of Montreal because ever since the days of the Northwest Fur Trading Company the west has been at a disadvantage; so many financial and industrial corporations were based in Montreal.
One need only look at the performance of CNR and Air Canada to realize how poorly institutions with head offices in Montreal serve western Canada even though they may be serving eastern Canada adequately. But when it comes to private corporations the government should at least refrain from coercing them to remain in an environment where they cannot do the best for their shareholders. It is often said that corporations should be aware of what is in the national interest. In the case of Sun Life specifically, the projected move should not be made, on the ground that it would not be good for national unity. But this begs the question. Sun Life is a mutual company and its policyholders are also the shareholders. A policyholder in western Canada should surely have the right to make his voice heard if he feels the company would operate better in some other part of the country than at its present headquarters; and the directors surely have the right to move the company in accordance with the desire of its policyholders.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that head offices are not moved easily. Knowing the directors of Sun Life, one realizes they would probably be most reluctant, personally to leave a city in which the company has been domiciled for a century or more. Incidentally, the suggestion has been made that Readers' Digest, which the government tried hard to move out of the country, may also move out of the Montreal area.
The language issue is a practical one. Statistics show that some 80 per cent of the financial operations of Montreal-based companies are carried on with English-speaking Canada or the United States. To conduct such a large portion of business in the other official language would undoubtedly put Sun Life at a serious disadvantage. For instance, it would make little sense to have a Sun Life policy written in Manitoba brought to Montreal and translated into French so that company employees could deal with it and then attempt to recommunicate with the Manitoba policyholder in their official language.
The attempt by the government to lean on Sun Life lends no strength, in the long run, to the movement for unity. It amounts to an attempt to force the company to do business under a set of conditions which it may find innappropriate; it might not be able to cope with such an environment and in the long run the policyholders are the losers. Should the savings of policyholders throughout the rest of Canada be poorly handled because of a government decree?
Some have suggested that Sun Life should be nationalized. I would remind hon. members that a mutual company, widely owned by many individuals, is very close to a co-operative. I cannot help thinking that many policyholders in the company will become uneasy about their savings as, indeed many Canadian investors are now starting to worry.

Bank Act
The failure of the government to deal with the Bank Act shows the low priority the government puts on our financial stability. It is suggested that the Sun Life confrontation with the Parti Quebecois in Quebec city has probably halted any early accessibility to markets there. Financial experts predict that Quebec may face additional problems in raising money in the European dollar markets. The New York market has already put premium prices on bonds from that province, and many traditional investors are staying clear of Quebec bonds.
The problem not only reflects on Montreal, it also reflects on the whole of this country, and it is certainly time this government faced up to these problems.One of the ways in which the government could help is to bring forward the amendments to the Bank Act so there can be a thorough discussion of the problems facing this country, and particularly its financial institutions.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me inform the minister from Outremont that I am going to speak about women.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext: Something you don't know anything about, Mr. Lalonde.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext:
It is interesting, Mr. Speaker, how that brings the other side to life. When I first came to parliament one of the first question I asked was when the Bank Act was to be reviewed. With my experience in the business community one area to which I felt I could perhaps bring some fresh light in parliament was in the area of the banking system of this country.
There are three areas in which I should like to see changes. The first is in the attitude, that has been very eloquently spoken about tonight, toward the small and owner-managed businesses in this country, where there needs to be a fresh and new approach. If 90 per cent of our small businesses employ less than 50 per cent of those employed, just think of what could happen if there was a fresh and enthusiastic response from the banking community toward those companies.
I should like also to speak of two other aspects of this situation, the first being the banking community's discrimination against women. The other, which disturbs me as well, is the fact that the banks in this country operate in very tall office blocks or glass houses far from the real world. For example, even our Department of Finance has to live in a rarified atmosphere 30 storeys up. We have this incredible glass house across the way. There is also that almost obscene situation in Toronto where all our banking establishments are bent on seeing which can build the tallest glass house.
What this country needs is a new attitude in the banking community. It does not need to go up. What the banking community needs to do is to spread out across this country and realize there are changes required and a vitality to be stimulat-

ed. The preoccupation of the banking community to build banking towers is just a disgrace.
This Bank Act review could do a great deal toward bringing a new economic era to this country if we had the time to talk about it. What sectors and what regions need to be provided for and promoted? Just think of what effects the provision of capital could have on the socioeconomic life of Canadians. How is money to be handled in the future by the banks as business transactions and as savings? There should be a fresh approach toward savings in this country and how our banks should operate in a post-industrialized society. We could have had such a fresh and good time in this parliament had we been able to examine these things.
One lesson I learned, and about which I tell school children when I speak to them about parliament, is the lesson I learned while sitting in that back bench last year. In that small corner in which I sat there were people from the mountains of British Columbia, from the tobacco farms of Ontario, from the ranching country of Saskatchewan; and next to me sat my two NDP colleagues, one from Vancouver and the other from Nickel Belt. What I learned sitting in that corner-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext: You must have learned a lot.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext:
Yes, I did learn a lot and I am very grateful. What I did learn was that in this House of Commons we speak for and understand all the constituencies in this country. Instead of the Bank Act being talked about in those ivory towers 30 storeys up, it should be brought here where people who know what is going on in this country might have some input.
Let me speak especially about the banking world and what is happening in that regard to women. We might have had meaningful discussions about discrimination in the financial community toward women. There is a great need to re-examine this whole area. In the past ten years many important changes have taken place in Canada, and this may have been one of the great social revolutions so far as women are concerned.
There are significantly more women seeking credit today, and this reflects the fact that more and more women are employed outside the home. We have taken initial steps to protect women against discrimination in the credit field, but the guidelines are voluntary and the credit situation is still unfair. Women's rights to equal access to credit have been denied through misconceptions regarding women's creditworthiness.
In the past when banks were rapidly expanding their share of the personal credit market some personal loans officers were, to use the banks' terms, a little over-cautious in granting credit. That is an understatement. Until 1968 the National Housing Act specified that when a financial institution was calculating how large a mortgage a family could handle it could only include 50 per cent of the wife's income in the total family income. These regulations were changed to remove the implication that the husband was the chief breadwinner, making it possible for the financial institutions to include any or all of the spouse's income in calculating a loan.
January 23, 1978

In 1971 additional changes stipulated that an applicant for an NHA mortgage could not be discriminated against on the basis of sex or marital status. It is fine to introduce guidelines and regulations, but we cannot ignore the fact that a vastly improved credit situation is still hiding great inequalities. Married women with incomes of their own are still being asked to provide information about their husbands' income on credit applications. It is still true that a newly separated, divorced or widowed woman does not enjoy equal opportunity for credit. In many cases such a woman will find that she has no credit identity separate from her husband's.
The two great bastions of discrimination against women are still senior sections of the federal government and the financial community. The minister from Outremont says he has been doing a great deal about this, but the 1976 statistics show that 70 per cent of all women in the federal service make less than $10,000 a year, while only 20 per cent of men earn less than $10,000 per year. Only 1 per cent of senior management jobs are held by women. I shudder to think what the statistics are in respect of the financial community, but those are the government's own statistics.
If women are to play a more important role in the business community, breakthroughs must come in two key areas, opportunities and access to capital. The same banks which are making strides in promoting women to positions of authority are refusing other women business loans. In my experience a woman president of a company was told that, had she been a man, her loan would have been twice as great. Many bank managers still adopt a negative attitude toward women borrowers. When asked for a business loan, the bank manager said: "Why does a nice little girl like you want to go into business?" That is another story which indicates that a bit of change is needed in the financial community.
An MBA student graduated from university last summer. He was employed in a local bank. He was told to make certain he opened a bank account in a neighbouring bank, because the bank did not want other women working in the bank to know what he was receiving. He has since left that bank.
The requirement that a husband sign a contract made by his wife for credit or a loan, and the issuance of credit cards only to a husband, are two practices which women find unsatisfactory and humiliating. Such policies presume that a married woman will have no income of her own. With the number of women now in the working force, this is no longer a valid assumption.
What share have women in high level decision-making in our corporations? Almost none. Women hold less than 1 per cent of the top corporate positions. The shortage of women is most marked in the fields of finance, mining and utilities. In the early 1970s the chartered banks had one woman director and no female corporate officer. In finance, trust, loans and insurance companies there were four women directors out of
Bank Act
697 and one female corporate officer out of 73. I think that is a great shame. Our women are qualified and well educated but they are not being afforded an opportunity to serve this nation. One would think that the federal government, after the great year of the women, would have seen to it that there were changes in our Crown corporations.
Recently I picked up the annual report of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and to my utter horror discovered there was not one woman director in that institution. I hope I have rectified the situation by submitting within 24 hours a list of capable women able to sit on the board of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet).

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext: But were they Liberals?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext:
I was very careful to make certain that half the list contained names of women who were Liberal.
I notice the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde) is not listening to what I am saying. The odds against a nonCanadian getting on a Canadian board of directors are six to one. The odds against a woman getting on a Canadian board of directors are 104 to one, in spite of the fact that 35 per cent of company shares usually are owned by women. It was Stephen Leacock who said: "When I go into a bank I get rattled." It might well not have been Leacock who said that but most Canadian women who seek credit in our banks. Of course, it was a wise woman who said it is a terribly difficult task being a woman, since it consists of dealing principally with men.
I am sorry we did not have an opportunity to bring before committee the many, many briefs from women who believe they should participate in the financial concerns of this country.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) saw fit to interject some remarks in this debate this afternoon, although he was not here when the bill was introduced. When the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) was speaking, the minister started belabouring him about certain facts. This was refreshing because we have not seen the minister for some time. One of the last times the minister appeared in Hansard was on December 7, 1977, when he was asked the following question by the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark):
Will the minister tell the House when he will be in a position to bring to parliament a specific proposal to embody that employment tax credit, when will it be before the House, and will we have it this month, as the Prime Minister promised?
As reported at page 1634 of Hansard, the minister replied as follows:
I will be able to come to the House with a statement seven days after Bill C-l 1 is passed.
Bill C-ll was passed on December 13, 1977. Seven days later would have been December 20, 1977. We have not heard his statement as yet. I will be patient. After all, we have waited 11 years in order to have another look at the Bank Act.

January 23, 1978
Bank Act
I suppose we can wait another day or so for the statement which the Minister of Finance promised in December.
This act was last in front of the House 11 years ago when it was revised. The revision provided that it be reviewed in ten years. One would think the government would consider ten years' notice to be sufficient, but it was unable to get ready a bill in that time. The government required another year, and today it has indicated that it needs yet another year. It is simply a measure of the incompetence of the minister and his staff when they cannot prepare a bill to review the Bank Act after approximately 11 years' notice.
I should like to spend a moment talking about the peculiarity of our banking system. I support the reference of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) to the Bank of British Columbia, and the help it has been to the business community having a bank with local interest. I was involved with a problem in my constituency when the Ogden Point pier burned down last August. We set up a committee of public servants, politicians and interested citizens in order to figure out a manner in which to reconstruct the docks, and particularly the warehouse on the docks, so that the business of loading and unloading pulp and paper could resume.
One innovation in the last ten years has been the quasi-bank supported by the federal government. I am referring to the Federal Business Development Bank and the Export Development Bank. These are not banks covered by the Bank Act, but they pass themselves off as banks in any event. The subject of our discussions at that time was how we could finance the reconstruction of the warehouse and the docks in Victoria. The cost was to be approximately $1.5 million. The federal government was unable to promise any help whatsoever, but a representative of the British Columbia Development Bank, when he was asked if he would back a loan to enable construction to go ahead, said he would.
I should like to refer to what has been happening in Cana-dair with respect to the LearStar aircraft program by referring to an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal, dated February 16, 1977. In part it reads as follows:
On December 2 of last year-
That would be December 2, 1976.
-Hugh Poulin, Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce Minister Jean Chretien, stated that Canadair estimates it will have to borrow up to $128 million in 1979 for the LearStar program.
Of this amount, he said, $128 million is to be provided by a consortium of two Canadian banks, and Ottawa will guarantee $50 million of the loan while Quebec will guarantee a further $20 million, the balance to be secured by a pledge of Canadair's assets.
The balance would be something in the neighbourhood of $58 million. The assets of Canadair are owned 100 per cent by the government. They were bought for $30 million. Another $8 million was dedicated when Canadair and the federal government got caught in the wrong in a suit laid against them by Northrop aircraft for the mishandling of its contract with them. The government saw fit to divert this $8 million to Canadair and claimed to be increasing its equity in a firm which was already owned 100 per cent by the government.

Surely the federal government is the only government in the world which owns 122 per cent of a firm. However, they will pledge these Canadair assets to cover the money that the banks are not going to cover.
This was the story of the Canadian banks: Two Canadian banks were supposed to form a consortium to provide that money. It was a rather familiar tale with this company because, hon. members will recall, there was supposed to be a Canadian consortium to find money for the LRPA contract. Now we find quite a different story in the January 6, 1978 issue of the Globe and Mail which stated:
The federal government has approved a proposal by Canadair Limited in Montreal, which is wholly owned by the government to raise $70 million (U.S.) in five year promissory notes in international capital markets for use in financing the development and production of the CL600 Challenger executive jet in Canada.
The international financing is to be arranged by Merrill Lynch International and Co., an affiliate of Royal Securities Ltd., of Toronto ...
At the same time, industry, trade and commerce minister Jack Horner has agreed to several undertakings related to the $70 million financing by Merill Lynch, including an agreement that if cost overruns occur in connection with the Challenger program, he will seek parliamentary authority for whatever additional funds are needed to permit Canadair to meet such unforeseen expenditures.
I suspect those unforeseen expenditures will arise as certainly as the sun will rise tomorrow. The Globe and Mail article goes on:
The government also agreed, as long as any of the $70 million in promissory notes is still outstanding, not to sell or transfer its ownership in Canadair or change its shares in such a way that the government's voting rights associated with its Canadair shares are reduced to less than 66.6 per cent or that the government no longer elects all of the members of Canadair's board of directors.
Let me point out two things. To date the directors on the Canadair board elected by the government are all senior civil servants, the majority of whom come from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Ottawa owns 100 per cent of the common and preferred shares in Canadair and they have guaranteed not to sell them. That is very strange when you consider the original reasons for their purchase of Canadair, which was to put Canadair together with the de Havilland company in Toronto to form a viable aerospace industry which would be attractive for some private company to buy. Now there is no longer any talk of putting together a viable package and selling the industry. They are saying now that they promise not to sell and that they remain committed to cover any overrun cost which might occur in the production and sale of LearStar jets.
I find that the banks of Canada are put in this position on a fairly regular basis by this government, which is the sole organization left in this country that can raise and control large amounts of capital. It is no wonder that banks are confused, and with the management this government provides, it is no wonder that banks are very hesitant to commit their own funds, particularly Canadian banks which know this government better than American banks do, although American banks have locked them into a pretty tough contract in order to provide another $70 million for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to get his favourite plane flying.
January 23, 1978

I have nothing further to add, Mr. Speaker. I am sorry that the government is too incompetent to bring in this bank bill of which they have had 11 years' notice. I trust the next government will be more competent. I want to point out that I think the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) is in a very poor position to predict what will happen at the end of five years to these promissory notes which they are selling in the United States, backed by the government. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce says he wishes to be remembered as a great friend of business, but he has about as much chance of being remembered as a friend of business as Benedict Arnold had of being remembered as the conqueror of Ticonderoga.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this bill because I think it is important. It indicates one of the weaknesses of this government in relation to the Bank Act, a weakness that has existed for a number of years. When the Bank Act was originally passed, we were to have a revision of the act every ten years. This has been delayed over a period of years now until one of these days we will miss the ten year period and a decade will have gone by with no revision. Although the government is now asking in this bill for the revision to be held over and for parliament to free the government of the responsibility to make changes that are required by law, we are actually talking about changes that should have taken place in 1970, and this is 1978. So we have had considerable slippage in following the provisions of the act for some time. I think one of the reasons for this is that the government is too busy worrying about a number of other problems.
It was interesting to note that the financial institutions are very influential, not only here but in other countries. I was particularly interested in some of the remarks that were made about the changes contemplated by Sun Life in its proposed move from Montreal because of certain conditions for which this government has been responsible for the last two or three years. Perhaps that is why the white paper with which we were presented has never been proceeded with.
It is interesting to note that there are a number of banks in this country which, as hon. members have said, are protected in such a way that they are guaranteed their savings, so that for many years no bank has gone bankrupt in this country. This is in contrast with the hundreds of thousands of banks operating in the United States which collapsed during the depression years. One of the reasons that Canadian banks are not in difficulty is the interrelationship between the Government of Canada and its banking institutions which allows the government to decide what the savings should be, what the margins of the banks should be and what banks may be developed. That control seems to me to have worked very well in protecting the banks but it has not always worked so well in protecting the public.
Much of our trouble in this country stems from the fact that while Canadians have much money in savings, in most instances they are reluctant to put that money into the development of our country, and particularly into the social
Bank Act
capital of our nation. When a municipality wants to raise money, it calls on the suitcase bankers to lend much of it. Suitcase bankers are not necessarily bad bankers. As was pointed out recently by one of my colleagues, very seldom is there a foreclosure or a mistake made by a U.S. suitcase banker who comes to this country, makes large loans and returns home, without having run any establishment in this country. We have been very particular in our relations with them. When a different government is formed, it does not matter in what province, a trip is always made to New York- although it does not always happen as fast as has been the case in the past year-to find out whether or not Wall Street will back the debentures or the requirements of the province. The state of the nation has had something to do with their ability to maintain or establish credit ratings which are so important to these suitcase bankers.
It behooves us to study banking in this country. Hon. members are aware that a finance company once came before parliament asking for permission to establish a bank under rules and regulations totally different from those in the present Bank Act. That request was made because the Bank Act was being held up, and it has been held up for approximately three years. Parliament had to consider that application and some changes in the Bank Act which were asked for by that finance company. The government promised that finance company that Bank Act legislation would pass two years ago. The government also promised it would pass last year. Through the efforts of some members of the other place, some of us were convinced that because the Bank Act legislation was going to meet the requirements of the co-operative movement, finance companies, trust companies and others who had gone part way into the banking structure, the requested legislation should be passed, and we now have another bank operating under conditions which are different from those under which other chartered banks operate. This new bank is allowed to exist pursuant to legislation which is anticipated but which has not been passed and may not be passed for a number of years. That bank now operates and has advantages which in my opinion are not available to other banks.
Small community development projects today are at the mercy of ordinary banks. We set up the Federal Business Development Bank, the old industrial development bank. It is supposed to be a bank of last resort, but people find that instead of making the concessions they have to make to the FBDB they might as well make them to ordinary banks.
There are some changes which should be made. We should be discussing the role of trust companies and co-operatives through their credit union and caisse populaire structure. We should be talking about the role of these institutions and whether it should be mandatory, as I presume is the case in the province of Quebec today, that regional consideration be given, and whether the same rules should necessarily apply in natural resource development areas as in the housing industry and in certain small businesses. Perhaps different rules should apply for exploration in the Arctic. There may be a strong argument

January 23, 1978
Bank Act
that we need to revise the Bank Act to take into consideration the diverse needs of communities.
It has always seemed odd-and this point has been dealt with many times by my colleagues in the Social Credit party-that Canada is not a leader in the field of lending institutions. We are certainly not, however, in the unenviable position of the United States where banks are asked to lend large sums of money to the international community, particularly developing countries. Ten years ago it was felt that if money was lent to those countries, those countries would develop their own resources and eventually become markets. In fact, that has not happened, and thus the International Monetary Fund finds itself in a very serious position. Although money was lent, the IMF has been unable to collect much of what is owing by the third world. Therefore the banking industry, particularly in the United States, is in great difficulty.
I am sure some Canadian banks are also suffering as a result of this, but they have not made loans of that kind to municipalities in Canada which desperately need capital to develop such things as educational systems or to provide sewers and water and other services. These are long-term projects, and they would be secure investments as long as the country remains secure.
Banks could have handled the financing of these kinds of projects. Interest rates could have been much lower; volumes would have been large. The first thing the newly elected premier of the province of Quebec did was go to Wall Street to see what terms he could obtain for borrowing for long-term development. That was also done by the premier of Saskatchewan. This would not be surprising if banking institutions in Canada were weak, but we have more savings per capita than any other country in the world. I was very amused to learn not long ago that we have $282 billion in insurance savings. If we have that amount lying around, we should not really need to go to another country to borrow money. Our banking structure should be such that through the Bank of Canada we could direct banks toward the type of lending in which they should be involved.
In revising the Bank Act we should consider two other matters which are closely connected. One of these has caused the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) to announce his retirement at the end of this parliament; that is, our competition legislation. That legislation is obviously a financial instrument, and it should be overhauled in such a way that a much more people-oriented direction could be taken so that not only companies but the public as well could be protected. Companies are certainly already well protected. If a company is bothered by competition, it can buy out that competition. The public must also be protected by our competition legislation, and money must be made available so that there can be competition.
My colleague spoke about the free enterprise system. He referred to the little corner hot dog stand and McDonald's sitting side by side. We say that this is a country of unlimited free enterprise where the little person can compete with

McDonald's. However, that is not the case at the bank, and if it is not the case at the bank, there really is no competition at all. There is no competition at the wholesalers, and if a small operation cannot get started with a loan bearing rates and conditions comparable to that enjoyed by McDonald's, that is not competition either.
A great deal of abuse has taken place with regard to bankruptcy, and this abuse has been suffered not so much by banks and financial institutions as by the public. Is there a constituency held by any hon. member in this House which has not experienced the bankruptcy of dozens of little companies? Secured creditors get their money when bankruptcies occur. Workers and suppliers of services and goods do not get any money. The only ones who get any money are financial institutions, and they do pretty well. Surely we must take these factors into consideration when dealing with the Bank Act. If we do not there will be a great deal of distrust resulting from the disparity that exists between large and small borrowers. Although the banks are quite happy to have small borrowers deposit their money, they are not so happy when they apply for loans.
The banking institutions have now entered the field of short term credit. I think there are few people who have not been offered some type of short term credit that will eventually end up in an Econocard or some such thing issued by a bank. I suggest there will be no such thing as money changing hands. The bank will get a note of your credits and deposits and will deal with withdrawals and other services by computer.
Few people who use banks today are unaware of the changes that have taken place in the banking community. I recently spoke to two bank managers from a community other than my own. It was interesting to hear them speak of a new problem: apparently the banks are being unionized. One mentioned that an employee had been made chief accountant, which was a new title. He did not get any more money, just the title. Mr. Speaker, what they are trying to do is put as many people as they can into management by giving them a title so that they will not be able to join a union. People in the banking world have no particular faith in their institutions and are well aware of how poorly many people are being treated.
I think it is high time we reviewed the Bank Act. Legislation should not be introduced the day before an election-which will probably take place in 1979-so that we will just get around at the last moment to putting in a ten-year change as a concession in order to get some thing done. Changing the Bank Act should involve all constituents of the banking community-trust companies, loan companies, the co-operative movement, caisses populaires and credit unions. Perhaps we should look at this question before we expand the activities of banks. I have always found banks to be identical, whether the Banque Canadienne Nationale or the Royal Bank.
If you approach several banks with a proposition you will likely get the same answer from them all; one will not take a chance any more than the other. If you approach a credit
January 23, 1978

union it will probably consider your character, your past record, whether you get along with your spouse and some other questions that indicate whether you are likely to remain in the community. Then they will probably make you a loan. There is no competition in banking. We must consider whether we have too many banks already or whether we should promote all the near banks to the status of regular banks. We created a bank for the IAC and allowed special considerations to their directors which were not available to any other bank.
We should approach the other place to do a serious study with whatever independence they retain. The chairman of the banking committee in the other place, Senator Hayden, probably holds many directorships in banking institutions. My hon. friend says not. The last time I looked he had five or six directorships and is connected with many other financial institutions. That may not be a bad thing, of course, because it may give him an insight into the institutions that the rest of us do not have. I would find it a very difficult problem, however, if he were to exercise the jurisdiction he gets from his directorships when making decisions in the other place. He made them in the case of IAC and I suggest he may make them for other banking institutions. This is a problem we should look at before the provinces decide to set up their own banks or before cities like Toronto decide to set up banks to serve their own needs. This would only further fragment the banking community and its ability to raise large sums of money for the development of some of the important interests of the nation.
The government should stop worrying about Quebec and get on with running the country. I think it is a cop-out to put this Bank Act off for another year. If there is no election then they will put it off for a further year. There are very serious problems in the banking institutions of this country. They have the ability to extend credit where it sometimes should not be extended, and they have the ability to withhold credit in the areas of housing and community development where it should not be withheld.
I think it is a very serious matter to put off the decennial review of the Bank Act. Instead of reviewing it in 1970, we are postponing it until 1978. We may well lose ten years through this remission we are granting now.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION TO APRIL 1, 1979
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to miss this opportunity during consideration of Bill C-16 to express once more my views about the Canadian monetary system which, in my opinion, ought to be modified. It should be amended so as to meet the needs of the population instead of being the master of the economic and financial situation in Canada. Mr. Speaker, I think we have often stated our position on that matter, that monetization of the nation's credit should be done through an institution exclusively owned by the state. I would not want someone to believe that I hold a grudge against bankers.
Certainly not; I respect them as human beings and I want them to do their job in our country, but I would like the
Bank Act
legislation under which they operate to be amended. The last time the Bank Act was revised, the Canadian parliament gave them more power. The interest ceiling was removed. They were given access to mortgage loans. While many industries are having great difficulty in surviving and saving their business because of competition from foreign products or on the international market, our banking institutions are making a lot of money because the legislation gives them special protection.
They never made as much profit as during the last few years when we have been plagued by serious inflation and high unemployment, which, far from decreasing, is going up according to the statistics, and it grieves us to repeat this. I would much prefer to be able to say this evening that the employment situation is improving in my constituency, that there are fewer unemployed, that more industries are being developed and can offer employment to the young people who graduate from our colleges, our CEGEPs, our universities and trade schools. I would much prefer to be able to say this, but because of somewhat peculiar circumstances, 1978 may be even worse than 1977. At the end of the year, if we look at the statements of chartered banks, we shall see once again that their profits have increased and that they have made more money while the other economic sectors are having an extremely difficult time.
Mr. Speaker, are we to believe that the government and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) are not aware of this? Is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) not aware of this? They are aware of this situation, but they are the lackeys of the financial powers, and the Prime Minister himself stated in 1977 that bankers were the worst complainers in Canada. It is because he is aware of the situation that he said this. He said that under his administration, the banks had made more profits than any other economic sector in Canada and that he was ashamed of this situation. Our right hon. Prime Minister said this. This was published in a magazine. All Canadians can read about that and I am sure that when the Prime Minister made that statement he knew what he was saying because he was acquainted with the facts.
Mr. Speaker, surely it does not rest with a single man to give up that authority or that constraint. It rests with Parliament and parliamentarians to help the government and the Minister of Finance to present legislation aimed at removing some powers from chartered banks and at amending section 72 of the Bank Act. I had hoped that during this session the government would introduce legislation to review entirely the Bank Act, but I realize that such is not the government intention. Bill C-16 is quite short since it is only two pages long.
In fact, there is only one clause, but a very important one, which further extends for months the supremacy of chartered banks on the minting of the nation's credit. I was discussing that matter with a former bank manager just before I came to the House and we were deploring the fact that such a section should give so much power to those financial institutions and that the Bank of Canada which is the bank of Canadians should have so little power compared with chartered banks.

January 23, 1978
Bank Act
We agreed that money is an instrument of exchange and measure of assets and that such an instrument should be totally under the authority of the government through the Bank of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, when it is suggested that Canada's money supply is created by the Bank of Canada, people are not being told the truth because of Canada's money supply which stands at about $100 billion the government of Canada through the Bank of Canada only created about 10 per cent of that. So who created the other 90 per cent of that money supply? Where does that money come from? Where does that money supply come from, if not through the creation of bank deposits made by chartered banks to their clients? And when their clients pay back the loans that were made to them through the creation of deposits, money is being destroyed. That is not the way it should be, Mr. Speaker. In this country that it not the way it should be if we really want to use our monetary system for the benefit of the people as a whole, the benefit of government and, as the hon. member who spoke before me suggested, provincial, municipal and school governments so those governments will be able to achieve objectives within their jurisdictions, provide people with services at decent costs, not being forced to pay back $5 for every $1.
That is the case now in this country, and I urge hon. members to consider the situation very seriously; I think I have spoken about this in the House then I quoted a very particular case when the federal government through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation made a loan-it made several but I am quoting a very particular case-to the Quebec Housing Corporation to build 30 housing units. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation after obtaining the necessary money from the government, money that it obtained from chartered banks, lent $537,863 to the province of Quebec. Mr. Bourassa, an economist premier, was not economical; he was a professional economist and, good boy that he was, he signed an agreement with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation promising to reimburse $57,000 yearly, for 50 years, that is $5 for each $1 borrowed.
Now, far be it from me to want to shock anyone in this House but, in the province of Quebec we are living under another government, another premier. Are things any different? Again, Mr. Speaker, big finance is running the show, dictating its will to the new government of Quebec, deciding what it must and must not do. In other words, the financiers control the credit of the nation, they order the governments around, what we call democratic governments. That is financial dictatorship in parliamentary democracy and the nation is its laughingstock. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation whatsoever to say that I shall vote against Bill C-16 because I did not really expect that we could deal in depth and completely with the Bank Act, to really improve it and assign the monetary system its real role while allowing chartered banks to serve the private sector and serve it well.

I am not criticizing the accounting system of the banks because it is excellent. They have remarkable officers and they know how to take advantage of a law which serves them well. I would like this act to be amended in such a way that we can be proud to say that in Canada we have an exemplary monetary system, a monetary system which serves the private sector well but which does not dominate the public sector that should be ruled by the representatives of the people.
If we are elected for something, let us prove it, reject Bill C-16 and require the government to get on as soon as possible with the study of legislation with a view to revising the Bank Act and at that time we will debate in an objective manner and bring forward the necessary amendments to this bill so that the Bank of Canada may truly become the bank of Canadians and that it may lend to the chartered banks the necessary credits in proportion to their needs to further the development of our country. This would bring order to our financial system; two separate sectors: the public sector would be financed by the institution of all Canadians and the private sector would be financed by private financial institutions. If we do not come to such a solution, I am convinced that within five, ten or 20 years Canada's debt which has doubled within the past eight years, the gross national debt which amounted to $43 billion in 1968 and which has risen to $86 billion in 1976 will not diminish in the coming years but rather increase. The servicing of the debt will also increase.
The government will either have to again borrow billions of dollars or increase its levies on Canadian taxpayers in order to pay the interest to those who control the minting of the credit in our country. At that time, we will realize that we are facing a tremendous national debt. According to accounting experts we are now indebting ourselves to the tune of $16,000 a minute. In the present budget, it is costing us more than $15 million a day just in interest on the Canadian public debt, and that excludes municipal or provincial debts.
Is that a good system? Let us keep it if it is any good. But then let us stop complaining and I am convinced that if we keep it, our private enterprise system, our capitalist system which should be the best in the world because it should be more likely to represent the aspirations of free men is going to crumble very quickly, because we have asked too much of it. If we refuse to bring about reforms, to correct our system which is increasingly degenerating, one of these days we will wake up to the realization that it is impossible to make this private enterprise system survive and we will then enter an era of dictatorship that nobody wanted in the first place but that we will be compelled to suffer because we will not have had the courage to take up to our responsibilities while it was still time.
This is why very briefly I wish to state again very clearly my position. I still think, like our party, that we should revamp our monetary system and make changes to it. Yet only parliament has authority on that matter and cabinet members, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) under the direction of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have the authority, according to our procedure, to present such a legislation. We
January 23, 1978

can talk about it and make representations but the final decision will be made by the members of cabinet. Then, if cabinet members bring the legislation that will correct the situation 1 shall be the first to say that owing to them, to the cabinet, to those men who had the guts to confront big finance, to put some order in, if we have good results, 1 shall recognize that owing to them we have at last a monetary system serving the Canadian people.
